It can result from prolonged rainfall, intense thunderstorms, rapid snowmelt, overflowing rivers, or drainage systems becoming overwhelmed. Flooding can develop gradually over several days or occur suddenly with little warning. Provo's location between the Wasatch Mountains and Utah Lake creates several potential flooding hazards. Snowmelt and heavy precipitation can increase flows in the Provo River and other waterways, while steep mountain terrain can channel runoff rapidly toward developed areas. Low-lying neighborhoods and locations with limited drainage capacity may be especially susceptible to flooding. Flooding can damage homes, businesses, roads, bridges, and underground utilities. Rising water can make transportation routes impassable, overwhelm stormwater infrastructure, and threaten public safety. Significant flooding may require evacuations and disrupt essential services while damaged infrastructure is repaired. Local Example2013 — Provo Flooding On September 7, 2013, intense thunderstorms flooded homes, roads, and public areas in Provo. Runoff washed out part of Grand Avenue near 900 North. About Flooding × Types of Flooding​ Flooding can occur through several different processes: River Flooding: Occurs when water levels rise above the banks of a river or stream, inundating surrounding land. Prolonged rainfall and melting snowpack can increase river flows beyond the capacity of the channel. Flash Flooding: Develops rapidly, often within minutes or hours of intense rainfall. Flash floods can produce powerful currents with little warning, particularly in mountainous terrain, narrow canyons, and urban areas. Snowmelt Flooding: Occurs when rising temperatures cause accumulated snow to melt faster than rivers, streams, and drainage systems can accommodate the resulting runoff. Rapid warming or rainfall on an existing snowpack can increase the risk. Urban Flooding: Occurs when rainwater accumulates on streets, parking lots, and other developed surfaces because storm drains and drainage channels cannot carry it away quickly enough. How Flooding Develops​ Flooding occurs when water enters an area faster than the surrounding environment or drainage infrastructure can accommodate it. Several factors influence how quickly floodwaters accumulate: Precipitation Intensity: Heavy rainfall over a short period can overwhelm drainage systems and cause rapid runoff. Soil Saturation: When soil is already saturated, less additional water can infiltrate the ground, increasing surface runoff. Snowpack and Temperature: Rapid warming can release large volumes of water stored in mountain snowpack, increasing streamflow. Topography: Steep slopes accelerate runoff, while valleys and low-lying areas can concentrate accumulating floodwaters. Urban Development: Roads, buildings, and paved surfaces reduce the amount of water that can soak into the ground, increasing runoff into stormwater systems. These factors can combine, causing flooding even when precipitation occurs outside the area ultimately affected. Understanding Floodplains​ A floodplain is an area of land adjacent to a river, stream, or other waterway that may become inundated when water levels exceed the normal channel. Floodplains are a natural part of river systems. During periods of high flow, water spreads beyond the riverbanks into surrounding low-lying areas. Development within floodplains can increase the potential for damage when flooding occurs. Floodplain maps identify areas with modeled flood hazards and help communities understand where significant flooding may occur. However, flooding is not limited to designated floodplains. Heavy rainfall, drainage failures, and localized runoff can cause flooding in areas outside mapped flood zones. Understanding the 100-Year Flood​ Flood risk is often described using statistical probabilities. A 100-year flood does not mean that a flood occurs only once every 100 years. Instead, it describes a flood magnitude with a 1% chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year. Common flood probability classifications include: Flood Classification Annual Probability 10-Year Flood 10% 25-Year Flood 4% 50-Year Flood 2% 100-Year Flood 1% 500-Year Flood 0.2% Each year's probability is independent of previous years. Therefore, a 100-year flood could occur in consecutive years or multiple times within a relatively short period. Over a 30-year period, an area exposed to a 1% annual-chance flood has approximately a 26% chance of experiencing at least one flood of that magnitude or greater, assuming the annual probability remains constant. Understanding these probabilities helps explain why significant flooding remains possible even in locations where major floods are relatively uncommon. Learn More: National Weather Service — Flood Hazards LikelihoodLikely MagnitudeCritical Potential Impacts Health & Safety Housing & Displacement Buildings & Infrastructure Transportation Communications Risk Map Landslide More Info Landslides occur when soil, rock, or other earth materials move downhill under the influence of gravity. They develop when the forces pulling material downslope exceed the strength holding it in place. Landslides can occur suddenly or develop gradually, with some continuing to move over months or years. Provo's location along the Wasatch Mountains creates areas of elevated landslide susceptibility, particularly along steep foothills and slopes containing unstable geologic materials. Groundwater, heavy precipitation, erosion, and changes to natural slopes can contribute to instability. Previous landslide activity in developed neighborhoods demonstrates that these hazards are not limited to undeveloped mountainsides. Landslides can damage or destroy homes, roads, retaining walls, and underground utilities as the ground shifts beneath them. Even slow movement can crack foundations, distort structures, and compromise essential infrastructure. Significant landslides may force evacuations, restrict access to neighborhoods, and create costly, long-term recovery challenges. Local Example2005 — Sherwood Hills Landslide Following an unusually wet winter in 2005, increased groundwater contributed to renewed landslide movement in Provo’s Sherwood Hills neighborhood, damaging homes and infrastructure. Some homes were condemned. About Landslide × How Landslides Occur​ Gravity continuously pulls soil and rock downhill. Under stable conditions, the strength of the earth materials and the friction between them resist this movement. A landslide occurs when the forces pulling material downhill become greater than the forces holding the slope in place. This can happen when a slope becomes overloaded, its supporting material is removed, or the strength of the underlying soil and rock decreases. Water is one of the most important factors influencing slope stability. As groundwater accumulates, it can increase the weight of slope materials and reduce the friction and strength that help keep them in place. Types of Landslides​ Landslides can take several forms depending on the materials involved and how they move: Rotational Slides: Soil or rock moves along a curved failure surface, often causing the upper portion of the sliding mass to tilt backward. These movements can create steep scarps and uneven ground surfaces. Translational Slides: Material moves downhill along a relatively flat or planar surface. Large sections of soil or rock may shift together while remaining partially intact. Rockfalls: Individual rocks or larger rock masses detach from steep slopes or cliffs and fall, bounce, or roll downhill. Rockfalls can occur rapidly and travel considerable distances. Slope Creep: Extremely slow movement of soil or rock downhill over long periods. Creep may gradually deform roads, fences, retaining walls, and building foundations. The speed and scale of landslide movement can vary greatly. Some landslides move only a few inches over several years, while others can travel downhill in seconds. What Triggers Landslides?​ Several natural and human-related factors can cause slopes to become unstable: Heavy Precipitation: Rainwater infiltrates the ground, increasing soil moisture and groundwater pressure. Snowmelt: Rapid melting can introduce substantial amounts of water into hillsides, particularly following winters with significant snow accumulation. Groundwater Changes: Rising groundwater levels can reduce the strength of soil and rock, allowing existing landslides to reactivate. Erosion: Streams, runoff, or excavation can remove material supporting the base of a slope. Earthquake Shaking: Ground vibrations can temporarily increase forces acting on unstable slopes and trigger movement. Human Activity: Construction, grading, irrigation, excavation, and changes to drainage patterns can alter slope stability. Landslides often result from several contributing factors rather than a single cause. Understanding Slow-Moving Landslides​ Not all landslides occur suddenly. Some move gradually over months, years, or even decades. Slow-moving landslides can remain relatively stable for long periods before becoming active again when groundwater levels rise or other conditions change. As the ground moves, buildings and infrastructure can experience uneven displacement, causing: Cracks in foundations, walls, and pavement. Doors and windows to become misaligned. Retaining walls and fences to tilt or separate. Underground water, sewer, and utility lines to break. Roads and sidewalks to shift or buckle. The Sherwood Hills landslides in Provo demonstrate how repeated slope movement can affect developed neighborhoods over extended periods. Learn More: USGS — Landslide Types and Processes LikelihoodLikely MagnitudeCritical Potential Impacts Health & Safety Buildings & Infrastructure Transportation Utilities Communications Mudslides & Debris Flows More Info Mudslides and debris flows occur when water mixes with loose soil, rocks, sediment, and vegetation, creating a moving mass that travels downhill under the force of gravity. Unlike ordinary flooding, debris flows contain large amounts of solid material and can carry boulders, trees, and other heavy objects. These flows can develop rapidly and travel with tremendous force. Provo's steep foothills and mountain drainages create conditions where debris flows can occur, particularly following intense rainfall or wildfire. Areas below recently burned watersheds are especially vulnerable because vegetation loss and changes to soil conditions can increase runoff and erosion. Drainages along the eastern benches can channel debris toward developed neighborhoods. Debris flows can bury roads, damage or destroy buildings, overwhelm drainage systems, and sever underground utilities. Their combination of water, sediment, and large debris makes them especially destructive. Flows can develop with little warning, threatening residents and infrastructure located along drainage channels and at the base of steep slopes. Local Example2025 — Buckley Draw Debris Flow On August 27, 2025, intense rainfall over the Buckley Draw burn scar triggered a debris flow in southeast Provo. Mud and debris damaged buildings and roads. About Mudslides & Debris Flows × How Debris Flows Form​ Debris flows develop when loose earth materials become mobilized by water and begin moving downhill. Heavy rainfall can produce rapid runoff that erodes soil and picks up loose sediment, rocks, and vegetation. As more material becomes incorporated into the moving water, it can transform into a thick, debris-laden flow. Unlike ordinary streamflow, debris flows contain enough sediment and rock to behave as a dense, moving mixture. The concentration of solid material allows them to transport large objects that flowing water alone might not be able to move. Debris flows often travel through existing stream channels, gullies, and mountain drainages before spreading outward onto flatter terrain. Mudslides vs. Debris Flows​ Although the terms are frequently used interchangeably, they can describe different types of earth movement. Mudflows: Flows consisting primarily of water and fine-grained materials such as clay, silt, and mud. They generally contain fewer large rocks than typical debris flows. Debris Flows: Rapidly moving mixtures of water, mud, sand, gravel, rocks, and vegetation. They can carry large boulders and trees over considerable distances. Debris Avalanches: Extremely rapid movements of loose earth materials that may travel long distances down steep terrain, sometimes with relatively little water compared with debris flows. The term "mudslide" is commonly used to describe several types of moving mud or sediment, but debris flow is generally the more precise scientific term when referring to fast-moving mixtures of water and coarse material. Why Wildfires Increase Debris Flow Risk​ Wildfires can significantly change how water moves across a watershed. Under normal conditions, vegetation intercepts rainfall, root systems help stabilize soil, and organic material slows surface runoff. Following a wildfire, several changes may occur: Vegetation Loss: Burned vegetation provides less protection against rainfall and surface erosion. Reduced Soil Absorption: Fire can contribute to water-repellent soil conditions, reducing the amount of rainwater that infiltrates the ground. Increased Surface Runoff: Rainfall can move more rapidly across exposed slopes and into drainage channels. Sediment Mobilization: Runoff can pick up loose soil, ash, rocks, and other material, increasing the volume and destructive force of the flow. These conditions can allow relatively short, intense rainstorms to generate destructive debris flows. The risk is often greatest during the first rainy season following a wildfire, although elevated runoff and erosion hazards may persist as the landscape recovers. How Debris Flows Travel​ Debris flows behave differently from ordinary floodwater because they contain a high concentration of sediment and other solid materials. As a debris flow moves downhill, it may: Accelerate on Steep Slopes: Gravity increases the speed and momentum of the moving material. Follow Drainage Channels: Existing gullies and streambeds can concentrate and direct the flow. Increase in Volume: The flow can collect additional sediment, rocks, and vegetation as it travels. Spread onto Alluvial Fans: When a flow exits a narrow canyon and reaches flatter ground, it can spread outward and deposit large amounts of debris. Block or Change Drainage Paths: Accumulated debris can obstruct channels, redirecting subsequent water and sediment into new areas. These characteristics make debris flows particularly dangerous near canyon mouths and developed areas below steep mountain drainages. Understanding Debris Flow Mitigation​ Because debris flows can carry enormous amounts of sediment and rock, communities sometimes construct specialized infrastructure to reduce their impacts. Common engineering approaches include: Debris Basins: Designed to capture and temporarily store sediment and other debris carried downhill. Diversion Channels: Direct flows toward designated areas and away from vulnerable buildings. Deflection Berms: Earthen barriers that redirect moving material away from structures. Check Dams: Small barriers placed within channels to reduce erosion and retain portions of transported sediment. These structures can reduce damage but cannot eliminate the risk, particularly when flows exceed their engineered design capacity. Provo's Buckley Draw watershed demonstrates both the effectiveness and limitations of debris flow mitigation. Following a 2002 wildfire, a diversion channel and protective barriers were constructed in 2003. These structures helped contain the 2003 mudflow and continued to provide protection during the much larger 2025 event, although portions of the 2025 flow exceeded the available protective capacity. Learn More: USGS — Post-Fire Flooding and Debris Flow Local Study: Provo City — Buckley Draw Debris Flow Forensic Study LikelihoodNot Rated MagnitudeNot Rated Potential Impacts Health & Safety Buildings & Infrastructure Utilities Transportation Sinkhole More Info Sinkholes are depressions or openings in the ground that form when underlying material can no longer support the surface above it. They commonly develop when groundwater gradually dissolves soluble bedrock, creating underground voids that may eventually collapse. Sinkholes can form slowly over many years or appear suddenly when the ground gives way. In Utah, natural sinkholes are associated primarily with areas containing soluble rock formations such as limestone, gypsum, and salt. Sinkholes are not identified as a major Provo-specific hazard in the regional mitigation plan, although localized ground collapse can occur where underground erosion or other subsurface conditions remove support from the ground above. Sinkholes and other localized ground collapses can damage buildings, roads, sidewalks, and underground utilities. Sudden collapses can create dangerous openings in developed areas, while gradual ground movement may cause foundations and pavement to crack or settle. The severity of damage depends on the size, depth, and location of the collapse. Regional ExampleHole-in-the-Ground Sinkhole, Utah Hole-in-the-Ground is a natural sinkhole in Utah formed by collapse of subsurface material. About Sinkhole × How Sinkholes Form​ Most natural sinkholes develop through a geological process known as dissolution, in which water gradually dissolves certain types of bedrock. Rainwater absorbs small amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil, forming a weak carbonic acid. As this water moves underground, it can slowly dissolve susceptible rocks such as limestone. Over time, several changes may occur: Rock Dissolution: Groundwater gradually dissolves portions of the underlying bedrock. Cavity Formation: Small fractures and openings expand into larger underground spaces. Loss of Support: The material above the cavity becomes increasingly unstable as the void grows. Ground Collapse: When the overlying material can no longer support its own weight, it may settle or collapse into the cavity. This process can take hundreds or thousands of years, although the final collapse may occur suddenly. Landscapes shaped by the dissolution of soluble bedrock are known as karst terrain. Types of Sinkholes​ Geologists generally recognize three common types of natural sinkholes: Dissolution Sinkholes: Form where soluble bedrock is exposed or covered by only a thin layer of soil. Water gradually dissolves the rock, creating shallow depressions at the surface. Cover-Subsidence Sinkholes: Develop when loose sediment gradually moves downward into openings within the underlying bedrock. These sinkholes typically form slowly and may produce broad, shallow depressions. Cover-Collapse Sinkholes: Occur when a layer of cohesive soil or sediment temporarily bridges an underground cavity before suddenly collapsing. These events can create deep, steep-sided holes with little visible warning. The type of sinkhole that develops depends on the underlying geology, groundwater conditions, and characteristics of the overlying soil. Natural vs. Human-Caused Ground Collapse​ Not every sudden opening in the ground is a geological sinkhole. Ground collapse can also result from human activity or failures in underground infrastructure. Examples include: Underground Erosion: Flowing water can transport soil through underground openings, gradually creating voids beneath the surface. Broken Water or Sewer Lines: Leaking pipes can wash away surrounding soil, removing support beneath roads, sidewalks, or structures. Underground Excavation: Abandoned mines, tunnels, or other subsurface excavations can collapse when supporting materials deteriorate. Groundwater Withdrawal: Lowering groundwater levels can contribute to subsidence or trigger collapse in areas already susceptible to sinkhole formation. Although these processes can produce similar surface damage, their underlying causes differ. A pavement collapse caused by a broken water main, for example, is not necessarily a natural geological sinkhole. Sinkholes in Utah​ Utah contains several types of soluble bedrock, including limestone, gypsum, and salt deposits. Where groundwater interacts with these materials, dissolution can create underground cavities and surface depressions. One documented example is Hole-in-the-Ground in Snake Valley, Millard County. This natural sinkhole formed in limestone bedrock and provides a visible example of how underground dissolution can produce a large surface collapse. However, sinkhole susceptibility varies considerably across Utah and depends on local geology. The presence of sinkholes elsewhere in Utah does not necessarily indicate that similar conditions exist beneath Provo. Learn More: USGS — Sinkholes Utah Example: Utah Geological Survey — Hole-in-the-Ground, Snake Valley LikelihoodHighly Likely MagnitudeLimited Potential Impacts Health & Safety Transportation Communications Public Services Avalanche More Info Avalanches occur when a mass of snow suddenly breaks loose and moves downhill under the force of gravity. They develop when the forces pulling snow downslope exceed the strength holding the snowpack together. Avalanches can travel at high speeds, carrying enormous amounts of snow and debris down mountain slopes. Provo's proximity to the Wasatch Mountains creates significant avalanche hazards in nearby mountainous areas, particularly Provo Canyon and the surrounding high-elevation terrain. Heavy snowfall, wind, changing temperatures, and steep slopes can create unstable snow conditions. Although most developed areas of Provo are not directly exposed, nearby mountain roads and recreational areas can be vulnerable. Avalanches can bury or injure people, damage infrastructure, and block transportation routes. Large avalanches may deposit substantial amounts of snow and debris across roadways, temporarily isolating communities or restricting access through mountain corridors. Avalanche hazards can also complicate emergency response and transportation during severe winter conditions. Local Example2024 — Rock Canyon Avalanche In February 2024, an avalanche crossed the Rock Canyon trail east of Provo, burying part of the trail and a bridge beneath deep snow. About Avalanche × How Avalanches Form​ An avalanche occurs when the force pulling snow downhill becomes greater than the strength holding the snowpack in place. Snow accumulates in layers throughout the winter. Each snowfall can create a new layer with different characteristics, including density, temperature, moisture content, and crystal structure. Some layers bond strongly together, while others contain weak or poorly bonded snow crystals. When a stronger, cohesive layer of snow rests on a weaker layer, the snowpack can become unstable. If the weak layer fails, the overlying snow may fracture and slide downhill. Four important ingredients contribute to many avalanches: Snow: Enough accumulated snow to form a moving mass. Slope: Terrain steep enough for gravity to pull the snow downhill. Instability: Weak layers or insufficient bonding within the snowpack. Trigger: An additional force or change that causes the unstable snow to release. Different avalanche types can form through different processes, but all involve snow moving downhill under the influence of gravity. Types of Avalanches​ Avalanches are classified according to how the snow releases and the characteristics of the moving material. Slab Avalanches: Occur when a cohesive layer of snow fractures and slides over a weaker layer beneath it. Slab avalanches can release across large areas and are responsible for most fatal avalanche accidents. Loose Snow Avalanches: Begin at a single point and spread outward as they move downhill, creating a fan-shaped path. They occur when loose, unconsolidated snow loses its stability. Wet Snow Avalanches: Develop when liquid water weakens bonds between snow grains. They are often associated with warming temperatures, rain, or melting snow. Dry Snow Avalanches: Involve relatively dry snow and can move rapidly, sometimes producing large airborne clouds of snow particles. These classifications can overlap. For example, a slab avalanche may involve either wet or dry snow. What Triggers Avalanches?​ Snowpack stability can change rapidly as environmental conditions evolve. Common contributing factors include: Heavy Snowfall: Rapid accumulation adds weight to existing snow layers, potentially exceeding their ability to support the additional load. Wind Loading: Strong winds transport snow from exposed slopes and deposit it on sheltered slopes, forming dense wind slabs. Temperature Changes: Warming and melting can weaken snow bonds, particularly when liquid water enters the snowpack. Rain on Snow: Rain adds weight and liquid water to the snowpack, potentially reducing stability. Human Activity: Skiers, snowboarders, snowmobilers, and other travelers can apply additional stress that triggers an unstable snow layer. Natural Releases: Avalanches can occur without direct human involvement when accumulated stress exceeds snowpack strength. In many avalanche accidents, the avalanche is triggered by the person involved or someone traveling nearby. Understanding Avalanche Terrain​ Terrain plays an important role in determining where avalanches begin and how far they travel. Most slab avalanches initiate on slopes between approximately 30 and 45 degrees, although avalanches can occur on steeper terrain. Important terrain characteristics include: Slope Angle: Slopes steeper than about 30 degrees are more likely to produce slab avalanches when unstable snow is present. Slope Aspect: The direction a slope faces affects sunlight exposure, temperature, and wind-deposited snow. Elevation: Snow accumulation, temperature, and wind conditions can differ significantly between lower and higher elevations. Terrain Traps: Gullies, creek beds, and depressions can concentrate moving snow, increasing burial depth. Avalanche Runout Zones: Areas below avalanche starting zones where moving snow can travel and eventually accumulate. Avalanches can travel into relatively flat terrain below the slopes where they originate. Consequently, locations beneath steep slopes may still be exposed to avalanche hazards. Understanding Avalanche Control​ Transportation agencies and mountain communities use several techniques to reduce the risk that avalanches pose to developed areas. Common methods include: Controlled Avalanche Releases: Explosives or specialized systems are used to deliberately release unstable snow under controlled conditions. Snow Sheds: Protective structures built over roads to allow moving snow to pass above the roadway. Avalanche Fencing: Specialized barriers designed to stabilize snow accumulation or influence how snow is deposited. Temporary Road Closures: Roads may be closed during periods of elevated avalanche danger or while avalanche-control operations are underway. Monitoring and Forecasting: Weather observations, snowpack measurements, and avalanche forecasts help specialists evaluate changing conditions. Provo Canyon is an example of a transportation corridor where avalanche mitigation helps reduce the risk to motorists and maintain access through mountainous terrain. It develops when precipitation remains below normal levels over time, often compounded by high temperatures and increased evaporation. Unlike sudden disasters, drought typically develops gradually and may persist for months or years. Provo's water supply depends on precipitation, mountain snowpack, local springs, and groundwater resources. Reduced winter snowfall and prolonged dry conditions can decrease runoff, limit groundwater replenishment, and place additional pressure on available water supplies. Utah's naturally dry climate makes the region particularly sensitive to extended periods of below-normal precipitation. Drought can reduce water availability for homes, agriculture, businesses, and natural ecosystems. Extended dry conditions can lower reservoir levels, affect groundwater supplies, damage vegetation, and increase demand on existing water infrastructure. Severe drought may also result in water restrictions, economic losses, and long-term environmental impacts. Local Example2026 — Utah Drought Conditions Utah experienced drought conditions during 2026, with effects on water availability and vegetation across parts of the state. About Drought × How Drought Develops​ Drought occurs when an area receives less precipitation than normal over an extended period, creating a growing imbalance between water supply and demand. Several environmental factors influence how drought develops and intensifies: Reduced Precipitation: Extended periods of below-normal rainfall or snowfall decrease the amount of water entering rivers, reservoirs, and groundwater systems. High Temperatures: Warmer conditions increase evaporation from soil and surface water and can increase water loss through vegetation. Low Snowpack: Reduced mountain snowfall limits the amount of water available from spring and summer snowmelt. Soil Moisture Deficits: Dry soils can absorb precipitation that might otherwise contribute to runoff and streamflow. Water Demand: Agricultural, residential, commercial, and industrial water use can increase pressure on limited supplies. Drought severity depends on how much precipitation is missing, how long the shortage continues, and how water availability compares with demand. Types of Drought​ Scientists generally recognize four types of drought, each describing a different aspect of water scarcity. Meteorological Drought: Occurs when precipitation remains below normal for a particular region over an extended period. Agricultural Drought: Develops when insufficient soil moisture or irrigation water affects crops, livestock, and agricultural production. Hydrological Drought: Occurs when water shortages become evident in rivers, streams, lakes, reservoirs, and groundwater supplies. Socioeconomic Drought: Develops when water shortages affect the availability of goods and services, creating economic or societal impacts. These classifications are closely related. A prolonged meteorological drought, for example, can eventually develop into hydrological drought as reservoirs and groundwater supplies decline. Understanding Utah's Snowpack​ Mountain snowpack serves as one of Utah's most important natural water-storage systems. During winter, snow accumulates in the mountains, storing precipitation until temperatures rise during spring and summer. As the snow melts, water flows into rivers, streams, reservoirs, and groundwater systems, helping sustain water supplies during Utah's typically hot and dry summer months. Several snowpack characteristics influence the amount of water available: Snow Accumulation: The total amount of snowfall during the winter season. Snow Water Equivalent (SWE): The amount of liquid water contained within the snowpack if all the snow were melted. Snowmelt Timing: When snow begins melting and how quickly the stored water is released. Soil Moisture: Dry soils can absorb a significant portion of snowmelt before runoff reaches streams and reservoirs. Temperature: Warmer conditions can accelerate melting and increase water losses before runoff reaches storage systems. A winter with below-normal snowpack can create water supply challenges even if rainfall during other parts of the year remains relatively normal. How Drought Is Measured​ Drought severity is commonly communicated using the U.S. Drought Monitor, which evaluates precipitation, soil moisture, streamflow, and other environmental indicators. The monitor uses five categories: Classification Description D0 — Abnormally Dry Dry conditions that may precede or follow drought D1 — Moderate Drought Developing water shortages and vegetation stress D2 — Severe Drought Increased water shortages and agricultural impacts D3 — Extreme Drought Major water shortages and significant environmental impacts D4 — Exceptional Drought Widespread and potentially devastating drought impacts The categories reflect the relative severity of drought conditions rather than a fixed amount of missing rainfall. D0 represents abnormally dry conditions and is not classified as drought itself. Why Drought Can Persist​ The end of a dry period does not necessarily mean that all drought impacts disappear. Different parts of the water system respond to precipitation at different rates. Soil Moisture: Rainfall may improve surface soil conditions relatively quickly, depending on the severity of the deficit. Streams and Rivers: Streamflow may recover when rainfall and snowmelt increase, although recovery depends on watershed conditions. Reservoirs: Large reservoirs may require multiple seasons of above-normal runoff to recover from significant deficits. Groundwater: Aquifers can respond much more slowly because replenishment depends on water gradually infiltrating underground. As a result, meteorological drought may end before hydrological drought conditions have fully recovered. Repeated dust storms can remove fertile topsoil, damage agricultural land, and contribute to widespread environmental degradation. Unlike an isolated dust storm, a Dust Bowl involves persistent conditions affecting an extensive region. Utah's arid climate, exposed lakebeds, and desert landscapes create conditions where wind erosion and dust storms can occur. Strong winds can transport dust into Utah Valley from distant source regions, particularly during dry periods. However, Provo is not identified as having a major Dust Bowl hazard in the regional mitigation plan. Severe dust storms can reduce visibility, disrupt transportation, and introduce large amounts of airborne particulate matter. Prolonged wind erosion can also degrade soil quality, damage agricultural resources, and reduce vegetation cover. These impacts can extend beyond the areas where dust originates, affecting communities many miles downwind. Regional Example1935 — Grantsville Dust Bowl During the 1930s, prolonged drought and overgrazing contributed to severe dust storms around Grantsville, Utah. In 1935, an especially intense dust storm killed livestock and threatened the community. Conditions became so severe that federal soil conservation efforts began in 1938. About Dust Bowl × How Dust Bowl Conditions Develop​ Dust Bowl conditions occur when environmental and land-use factors combine to make large areas of soil vulnerable to wind erosion. Several conditions contribute to their development: Prolonged Drought: Extended dry conditions reduce soil moisture and weaken vegetation that normally protects the ground. Vegetation Loss: Without grasses, crops, and other plants, the soil becomes more exposed to wind. High Winds: Strong or persistent winds can dislodge and transport loose soil particles. Soil Disturbance: Intensive cultivation, overgrazing, and other land disturbances can reduce soil stability and increase erosion. When these conditions persist, wind can repeatedly remove topsoil faster than it is naturally replaced. How Wind Erosion Works​ Wind erosion occurs when moving air lifts or pushes soil particles across the ground. Scientists generally describe three methods of soil transport: Suspension: Very small particles, such as dust and fine silt, become airborne and can travel hundreds or thousands of miles. Saltation: Sand-sized particles bounce along the ground as wind lifts them briefly before they fall back to the surface. Surface Creep: Larger particles roll or slide along the ground, often after being struck by bouncing particles. These processes can occur simultaneously, gradually removing soil from exposed landscapes. Fine airborne particles can remain suspended long after a dust storm has passed its original source area. Dust Storms vs. Dust Bowls​ Although closely related, dust storms and Dust Bowl conditions are not the same. Dust Storm: A weather event in which strong winds lift large amounts of dust or sand into the atmosphere, reducing visibility and potentially affecting air quality. Dust Bowl: A prolonged environmental condition characterized by repeated dust storms, widespread soil erosion, drought, and extensive land degradation. A single dust storm may last only minutes or hours, while Dust Bowl conditions can persist for years. Dust storms can occur without a Dust Bowl, particularly in desert regions and areas with exposed dry lakebeds. The Dust Bowl of the 1930s​ The most famous Dust Bowl occurred across portions of the Great Plains during the 1930s. During the preceding decades, extensive areas of native grassland had been converted into farmland. When severe drought developed, crops failed and large areas of exposed soil were left vulnerable to powerful winds. Repeated dust storms carried enormous quantities of topsoil across the region. Some storms transported dust across much of the United States, reaching the East Coast. The disaster caused widespread agricultural losses, economic hardship, and the displacement of thousands of farming families. The Dust Bowl demonstrated how prolonged drought, combined with unsustainable land management, can transform a regional environmental problem into a major disaster. It also contributed to the development of modern soil conservation programs and practices intended to reduce erosion and protect agricultural land. It develops when electrical charges build up within a storm and the difference between those charges becomes large enough to overcome the insulating properties of the surrounding air. Provo experiences thunderstorms, particularly during the warmer months when atmospheric instability and mountain terrain contribute to storm development. Lightning is especially relevant in exposed locations such as mountain trails, open fields, parks, and other outdoor areas. Lightning can also strike locations several miles from the heaviest rainfall. Lightning strikes can cause serious injuries or fatalities, ignite fires, and damage buildings, electrical equipment, and utility infrastructure. Electrical surges can disrupt power and communications systems, while strikes to trees or other objects can create additional hazards. Even relatively isolated lightning events can have significant consequences for individuals and affected facilities. Local Context2020 — Lightning Activity in Utah County A lightning detection report recorded 49,360 lightning pulses in Utah County on 55 days in 2020. The total includes in-cloud lightning, not just cloud-to-ground strikes. About Lightning × How Lightning Forms​ Lightning develops when electrical charges become separated within a thunderstorm. Inside a developing storm, strong upward and downward air currents cause ice crystals, supercooled water droplets, and soft hail particles known as graupel to collide. These collisions help transfer electrical charges between particles, causing different regions of the storm to develop positive and negative charges. Typically, positive charges accumulate near the upper portion of the storm, while negative charges become concentrated in the middle and lower portions. As the difference between these charges increases, the electric field becomes strong enough to overcome the insulating properties of the surrounding air. A conductive pathway begins to form, allowing a rapid electrical discharge to occur. This discharge is what we observe as lightning. Types of Lightning​ Lightning can occur in several different ways, depending on where electrical charges are released. Intracloud Lightning: Occurs between regions of opposite electrical charge within the same cloud. This is the most common type of lightning and often illuminates large portions of a thunderstorm. Cloud-to-Cloud Lightning: Occurs when an electrical discharge travels between two separate clouds containing regions of opposite charge. Cloud-to-Ground Lightning: Occurs when an electrical discharge connects a thunderstorm with the Earth's surface. This type presents a direct danger to people, buildings, trees, and infrastructure. Cloud-to-Air Lightning: Occurs when a discharge extends from a charged cloud into the surrounding atmosphere without connecting to another cloud or the ground. Some lightning appears as a broad flash illuminating an entire cloud. This is commonly called sheet lightning and usually results from lightning occurring within or behind clouds. Positive vs. Negative Lightning​ Cloud-to-ground lightning can transfer either negative or positive electrical charge. Negative Lightning: The most common type of cloud-to-ground lightning. It typically originates from negatively charged regions in the middle or lower portion of a thunderstorm. Positive Lightning: Less common and often originates from positively charged regions near the upper portion or anvil of a storm. Positive lightning can transfer substantial electrical charge and may strike farther from the main storm. Both types can cause serious injuries, fires, and infrastructure damage. Positive lightning is particularly noteworthy because it can occur well outside the areas experiencing heavy rainfall. Understanding Thunder​ Thunder is the sound produced by the rapid heating and expansion of air surrounding a lightning discharge. A lightning channel can heat the surrounding air to approximately 50,000°F (27,800°C), several times hotter than the surface of the Sun. This intense heating causes the air to expand explosively, creating a shock wave that travels outward as sound. Because light travels much faster than sound, lightning is usually seen before thunder is heard. The approximate distance to a lightning discharge can be estimated by counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder. Time Between Flash and Thunder Approximate Distance 5 seconds 1 mile 10 seconds 2 miles 15 seconds 3 miles 20 seconds 4 miles 30 seconds 6 miles This estimate provides only the approximate distance to the lightning discharge and does not establish whether a location is safe. Lightning Beyond the Storm​ Lightning does not always strike directly beneath the darkest clouds or heaviest rain. Some cloud-to-ground discharges travel horizontally away from a thunderstorm before descending toward the ground. These events are sometimes called bolts from the blue because they can strike areas beneath relatively clear skies. Lightning has been documented striking more than 10 miles from its parent thunderstorm, with some exceptional strikes traveling even farther. Consequently, lightning can threaten locations that are not experiencing rainfall or other obvious storm conditions. Learn More: National Weather Service — Understanding Lightning Additional Resource: National Weather Service — Bolts from the Blue LikelihoodNot Rated MagnitudeNot Rated Potential Impacts Health & Safety Transportation Buildings & Infrastructure Utilities Communications Heavy Rain More Info Heavy rain occurs when atmospheric conditions produce large amounts of precipitation over a relatively short period or sustained rainfall over an extended duration. It develops when moisture-rich air rises, cools, and condenses into clouds, allowing water droplets to grow until they become heavy enough to fall as rain. Intense thunderstorms can produce exceptionally high rainfall rates within a small geographic area. Provo's location along the Wasatch Mountains influences local precipitation patterns. Moist air can be lifted by mountain terrain, enhancing cloud development and precipitation under favorable conditions. Seasonal thunderstorms and occasional surges of monsoonal moisture can produce intense rainfall across Utah Valley, particularly during the warmer months. Heavy rainfall can overwhelm stormwater systems, reduce visibility, damage roads and infrastructure, and disrupt transportation and outdoor activities. Intense precipitation can also produce rapidly changing conditions across nearby communities, creating challenges for emergency response and infrastructure management. Local Example2025 — Heavy Rain at Buckley Draw On August 27, 2025, intense rain fell over the Buckley Draw burn scar in southeast Provo, triggering a debris flow that damaged nearby buildings and roads. About Heavy Rain × How Heavy Rain Forms​ Rain develops when moisture in the atmosphere condenses into cloud droplets that eventually grow large enough to fall toward the ground. Several atmospheric conditions contribute to heavy rainfall: Atmospheric Moisture: Water vapor provides the moisture needed for cloud formation and precipitation. Air containing more water vapor can support greater rainfall amounts when conditions are favorable. Rising Air: Air must generally rise and cool for water vapor to condense into cloud droplets. Atmospheric Instability: Warm, moist air rising through cooler surrounding air can produce strong upward currents and deep thunderstorm clouds. Sustained Moisture Supply: Continued movement of moist air into a storm can allow precipitation to persist or intensify. Inside clouds, tiny water droplets grow through collisions and other processes. When droplets become large enough, they fall as precipitation. Heavy rainfall can occur when storms produce precipitation efficiently or repeatedly affect the same location. Types of Heavy Rainfall​ Heavy rainfall can develop through several different atmospheric processes: Convective Rainfall: Produced by rising air within showers and thunderstorms. Convective storms can generate intense, localized rainfall over short periods. Stratiform Rainfall: Associated with widespread cloud systems that produce precipitation across large geographic areas. These events generally have lower rainfall rates than intense thunderstorms but can continue for many hours. Orographic Rainfall: Occurs when moist air is forced upward over mountains, cooling and producing precipitation. Monsoonal Rainfall: Associated with seasonal changes in atmospheric circulation that transport additional moisture into a region, often supporting the development of thunderstorms. These processes can overlap. For example, monsoonal moisture can fuel convective thunderstorms that are enhanced by mountain terrain. How Mountains Influence Rainfall​ Mountain ranges can strongly influence where precipitation develops and how much rain reaches the ground. When moist air encounters a mountain barrier, it may be forced upward along the terrain. As the air rises, atmospheric pressure decreases, allowing the air to expand and cool. If the rising air cools sufficiently, water vapor condenses into cloud droplets and precipitation may develop. This process is known as orographic lift. Several effects can occur: Enhanced Precipitation: Rising air can increase cloud development and precipitation along windward mountain slopes. Localized Storm Development: Mountain heating and terrain-driven air movement can contribute to thunderstorm formation. Rain Shadows: Air descending on the opposite side of a mountain range generally warms and becomes relatively drier, sometimes reducing precipitation. Variable Rainfall: Nearby locations can receive substantially different amounts of rain depending on elevation, storm movement, and terrain. The Wasatch Mountains influence weather patterns in Utah Valley, helping create differences in precipitation across relatively short distances. Rainfall Intensity vs. Accumulation​ Meteorologists evaluate rainfall using both its total accumulation and the rate at which it falls. Rainfall Accumulation: The total amount of precipitation received during a specified period, usually measured in inches. Rainfall Intensity: The rate at which precipitation falls, commonly expressed in inches per hour. For example: Rainfall Event Equivalent Average Rate 0.25 inches in 15 minutes 1 inch/hour 0.50 inches in 15 minutes 2 inches/hour 1.00 inch in 30 minutes 2 inches/hour 2.00 inches in 1 hour 2 inches/hour These examples demonstrate why rainfall duration matters. A storm producing one inch of rain in fifteen minutes has a much higher average rainfall intensity than a storm producing the same amount over several hours. The consequences of rainfall depend on the intensity, duration, and conditions of the affected area. Why Some Storms Produce Extreme Rainfall​ Certain atmospheric conditions allow storms to produce unusually large amounts of precipitation. Important factors include: Deep Atmospheric Moisture: Large amounts of water vapor provide additional moisture for precipitation. Strong Updrafts: Rising air can sustain thunderstorm development and support continued precipitation. Slow Storm Movement: A thunderstorm that remains over one location can produce large rainfall totals. Training Thunderstorms: Multiple storms move repeatedly over the same location, similar to train cars following the same track. Persistent Moisture Transport: Winds continually supply moist air to a developing storm system. Terrain Enhancement: Mountains can force moist air upward and intensify precipitation in favorable atmospheric conditions. These factors can combine to produce extreme rainfall rates and unusually large precipitation totals, sometimes affecting only a small portion of a larger region. Strong winds can develop from large weather systems, thunderstorms, or air flowing across mountainous terrain. Sudden gusts can produce damaging forces even when average wind speeds are relatively moderate. Provo's location along the Wasatch Mountains influences local wind patterns. Mountain slopes, canyons, and nearby valleys can redirect or accelerate airflow, sometimes producing strong downslope or canyon winds. Thunderstorms and passing weather systems can also generate powerful winds across Utah Valley throughout the year. High winds can uproot trees, damage roofs and buildings, overturn unsecured objects, and bring down power lines. Flying debris can threaten public safety, while damaged utility infrastructure may cause widespread power and communications outages. Severe wind events can also disrupt transportation and complicate emergency response. Local Example2006 — Provo Windstorm On August 1, 2006, severe thunderstorm winds damaged roofs, trees, and utility poles in Provo. A gust of up to 106 mph was reported in the affected area. About High Wind × How Wind Forms​ Wind is the movement of air caused primarily by differences in atmospheric pressure. Uneven heating of the Earth's surface creates differences in air temperature and density, contributing to areas of relatively high and low atmospheric pressure. Air accelerates in response to the pressure gradient force, which pushes air from higher toward lower pressure. Several factors influence the resulting wind: Pressure Gradient: Larger pressure differences over shorter distances generally produce stronger winds. Coriolis Effect: Earth's rotation deflects moving air, influencing wind direction over large distances. Surface Friction: Trees, buildings, and terrain slow winds near the ground and create turbulence. Topography: Mountains, valleys, and canyons can redirect and locally accelerate airflow. Wind speed and direction result from the combined influence of these forces. Types of High Wind Events​ Strong winds can develop through several different atmospheric processes: Gradient Winds: Winds associated with broad atmospheric pressure patterns. Strong pressure differences between weather systems can produce widespread windy conditions. Downslope Winds: Develop when air descends a mountain slope. Under certain atmospheric conditions, mountain waves can produce particularly strong and damaging winds near the base of a range. Canyon Winds: Winds influenced by airflow through mountain canyons. Local pressure and temperature differences, combined with terrain, can produce strong winds near canyon mouths. Thunderstorm Outflow: Winds produced when cooler, denser air descends within a thunderstorm and spreads outward after reaching the ground. Downbursts: Concentrated areas of strong descending air within thunderstorms. When the air reaches the surface, it spreads outward and can produce damaging straight-line winds. These processes can occur independently or combine to increase local wind speeds. How Mountains Influence Wind​ Mountainous terrain can significantly alter the speed and direction of airflow. Along the Wasatch Front, strong winds can develop when atmospheric conditions force air across the Wasatch Mountains and down toward the valleys. Several processes can influence wind behavior near mountains: Downslope Acceleration: Air flowing over mountain ridges can accelerate as it descends under favorable atmospheric conditions. Mountain Waves: Stable air flowing across a mountain range can develop wave-like motions. Some mountain-wave patterns produce powerful descending winds on the leeward side. Canyon Channeling: Terrain can concentrate and redirect airflow, sometimes increasing wind speeds near canyon entrances. Turbulence: Mountains, buildings, and other obstacles disrupt airflow, creating irregular changes in wind speed and direction. These effects help explain why wind conditions can vary significantly between locations only a few miles apart. Sustained Winds vs. Wind Gusts​ Wind is commonly described using two different measurements. Sustained Wind: The average wind speed measured over a specified period. The National Weather Service commonly uses a two-minute averaging period for surface observations. Wind Gust: A brief increase in wind speed above the prevailing average wind. Gusts may be considerably stronger than sustained winds. For example, a storm might produce sustained winds of 30 mph with occasional gusts reaching 60 mph. These short bursts can exert substantial forces on trees, roofs, signs, and other exposed structures. The force exerted by wind increases approximately with the square of its speed. This means that, under otherwise similar conditions, doubling the wind speed can produce roughly four times the wind pressure. Understanding Wind Speeds​ The Beaufort Wind Scale is a standardized system originally developed to describe wind strength using observable effects. It remains useful for understanding how different wind speeds can affect the surrounding environment. Wind Speed Beaufort Classification Typical Effects 13–18 mph Moderate Breeze Small branches move 19–24 mph Fresh Breeze Small trees begin swaying 25–31 mph Strong Breeze Large branches move 32–38 mph Near Gale Whole trees sway 39–46 mph Gale Twigs may break 47–54 mph Strong Gale Minor structural damage possible 55–63 mph Storm Trees may be uprooted 64–73 mph Violent Storm Significant wind damage possible 74+ mph Hurricane Force Potential for extensive damage These descriptions represent general wind effects rather than precise thresholds at which damage will occur. Actual damage depends on factors including exposure, building construction, tree condition, and wind duration. The National Weather Service generally classifies thunderstorm wind gusts of 58 mph or greater as severe. Learn More: National Weather Service — Wind Safety Additional Resource: National Weather Service — Beaufort Wind Scale LikelihoodHighly Likely MagnitudeNegligible Potential Impacts Health & Safety Buildings & Infrastructure Agriculture & Food Transportation Hail More Info Hail is a form of frozen precipitation consisting of balls or irregular lumps of ice that develop inside thunderstorms. Hailstones form when strong upward air currents carry water droplets into extremely cold regions of a storm, where they freeze and accumulate additional layers of ice. When the hailstones become too heavy for the storm's updrafts to support, they fall toward the ground. Utah County experiences thunderstorms capable of producing hail, particularly during the warmer months. Provo's location near the Wasatch Mountains can contribute to localized thunderstorm development when atmospheric conditions are favorable. Although most hailstorms produce relatively small hailstones, stronger thunderstorms can generate larger hail capable of causing significant damage. Hail can damage roofs, windows, vehicles, crops, and other exposed property. Larger hailstones can injure people and animals, while intense hailstorms may disrupt transportation and outdoor activities. Damage generally increases with hailstone size, impact speed, and the vulnerability of affected structures and materials. Regional Example2024 — Orem and Lindon Hailstorm On August 13, 2024, a thunderstorm produced hail reported up to 1.75 inches in diameter in nearby Orem and Lindon. About Hail × How Hail Forms​ Hail develops inside thunderstorms containing strong upward air currents known as updrafts. These updrafts carry water droplets into regions of the atmosphere where temperatures are below freezing. Some droplets remain liquid despite being below 32°F (0°C). These are called supercooled water droplets. When supercooled droplets encounter an ice particle, they freeze onto its surface, gradually increasing its size. Hail formation generally involves several stages: Initial Ice Formation: A small ice particle develops within a thunderstorm. Upward Transport: Strong updrafts carry the particle into regions containing supercooled water droplets. Ice Accumulation: Water droplets freeze onto the particle, increasing its size. Continued Growth: The hailstone may remain suspended or move through different regions of the storm, collecting additional ice. Descent: When the hailstone can no longer be supported by the updraft, it falls toward the ground. Some hailstones partially or completely melt while falling through warmer air below the thunderstorm. How Hailstones Grow​ Hailstones often contain multiple layers of ice, somewhat resembling the rings found inside an onion. These layers develop as hailstones encounter different temperature and moisture conditions while moving through a thunderstorm. Two important growth processes include: Dry Growth: Supercooled water droplets freeze almost immediately upon contacting the hailstone. Air bubbles may become trapped within the ice, producing a cloudy or opaque appearance. Wet Growth: Water collects on the hailstone's surface faster than it can freeze immediately. The water subsequently freezes, often forming clearer layers of ice. Alternating periods of wet and dry growth can create the distinct layered structure visible inside some hailstones. The number of layers does not necessarily indicate how many times a hailstone has traveled upward and downward through a thunderstorm. Understanding Hail Size​ The National Weather Service commonly describes hailstones by comparing their diameter to familiar objects. Hail Diameter Size Comparison 0.25 inches Pea 0.50 inches Marble 0.75 inches Penny 0.88 inches Nickel 1.00 inch Quarter 1.25 inches Half Dollar 1.50 inches Ping-Pong Ball 1.75 inches Golf Ball 2.00 inches Hen Egg 2.50 inches Tennis Ball 2.75 inches Baseball 4.00 inches Grapefruit 4.50 inches Softball The National Weather Service classifies a thunderstorm as severe when it produces hail at least one inch in diameter, wind gusts of at least 58 mph, or a tornado. Although smaller hailstones can cause damage, larger hail generally presents a greater threat to buildings, vehicles, and exposed property. Why Some Thunderstorms Produce Larger Hail​ The size of a hailstone depends largely on the conditions inside the thunderstorm. Several factors influence hail growth: Updraft Strength: Stronger upward air currents can support larger hailstones and allow additional time for ice accumulation. Supercooled Water: Greater amounts of available liquid water below freezing can support more rapid hailstone growth. Storm Organization: Long-lived, organized thunderstorms can maintain strong updrafts for extended periods. Temperature Structure: The depth of cold air within the storm and the amount of warm air below it influence hail growth and melting. Time Within the Storm: Hailstones that remain in favorable growth regions longer can accumulate additional ice. Particularly large hail is often associated with supercell thunderstorms, which contain persistent, rotating updrafts. These powerful updrafts can support hailstone growth for extended periods, allowing some stones to reach several inches in diameter. Hail vs. Sleet​ Although hail and sleet are both forms of frozen precipitation, they form through different processes. Hail: Develops inside thunderstorms when strong updrafts support the growth of ice particles through the accumulation of supercooled water droplets. Sleet: Consists of small ice pellets that generally form when snowflakes melt while falling through a layer of warmer air and then refreeze in a sufficiently deep layer of freezing air near the ground. Hail is most commonly associated with thunderstorms during warmer seasons, while sleet typically occurs during winter precipitation events. Unlike sleet, hail can form even when temperatures at the ground are relatively warm. Learn More: NOAA — Thunderstorm Hazards: Hail Additional Resource: NOAA — Hail Size Classifications LikelihoodHighly Likely MagnitudeLimited Potential Impacts Health & Safety Transportation Utilities Communications Public Services Heavy Snow More Info Heavy snow occurs when atmospheric conditions produce substantial accumulations of frozen precipitation over a relatively short period or through prolonged snowfall. Snow develops when ice crystals form within clouds and grow into snowflakes that reach the ground without completely melting. Heavy snowstorms can produce rapidly accumulating snow, reduced visibility, and significant disruptions to daily activities. Provo's location along the Wasatch Mountains creates conditions favorable for winter snowfall, particularly when moist air is lifted over mountainous terrain. Snowfall amounts can vary considerably with elevation, with mountain communities and canyon corridors often receiving substantially more snow than the valley floor. Winter storm systems can also produce significant accumulation throughout developed areas of Provo. Heavy snow can make roads impassable, disrupt transportation, damage trees and power lines, and interrupt essential services. Accumulated snow can place substantial weight on roofs and other structures, particularly when the snow is dense or contains significant moisture. Major snowstorms can restrict emergency vehicle access and delay the restoration of affected infrastructure. Local Example2010 — Heavy Snow in Provo On December 21, 2010, a Provo weather station recorded approximately 11 inches of snowfall in one day. About Heavy Snow × How Snow Forms​ Snow forms when water vapor in the atmosphere deposits onto tiny ice particles within clouds. As additional water vapor freezes onto these particles, ice crystals grow into different shapes depending on the surrounding temperature and moisture conditions. Under favorable conditions, individual ice crystals can collide and stick together, forming larger snowflakes. Snow formation generally involves several stages: Ice Crystal Formation: Water vapor deposits onto ice particles within sufficiently cold clouds. Crystal Growth: Additional water vapor accumulates, allowing ice crystals to grow. Snowflake Development: Individual ice crystals may combine into larger, more complex snowflakes. Descent: Snowflakes fall toward the ground as they become large enough to overcome upward air currents. Surface Accumulation: If snowflakes remain sufficiently frozen during their descent, they can reach the ground and accumulate. Snow can sometimes reach the ground even when surface temperatures are slightly above freezing, particularly when the warmer layer is relatively shallow and snowfall is intense. Types of Snow​ Snow can have very different physical characteristics depending on temperature, moisture content, and atmospheric conditions. Dry Powder Snow: Contains relatively little liquid-water equivalent for its depth. The snow is generally light, fluffy, and less densely packed. Wet Snow: Contains more liquid-water equivalent for a given depth and is typically denser and heavier. Wet snow can cling to trees, power lines, and other exposed surfaces. Compacted Snow: Develops when existing snow settles or becomes compressed. Compaction increases density and reduces snow depth without necessarily removing much of its water content. Crusted Snow: Forms when the upper portion of a snowpack melts and refreezes, creating a harder surface layer. These differences help explain why two snowstorms producing the same accumulation depth can have significantly different impacts. Understanding Snow-to-Liquid Ratios​ Snow-to-liquid ratio describes the relationship between the depth of accumulated snow and the amount of liquid water it would produce if completely melted. A commonly used approximation is a 10:1 ratio, meaning ten inches of snow would produce approximately one inch of liquid water. However, actual ratios can vary substantially depending on snow density. Snow-to-Liquid Ratio Snow from 1 Inch of Water General Description 5:1 5 inches Very wet, dense snow 8:1 8 inches Wet, heavy snow 10:1 10 inches Common approximation 15:1 15 inches Relatively dry snow 20:1 20 inches Light, fluffy snow These are illustrative classifications, not fixed thresholds. Snow density can vary within the same storm. For example, six inches of snow with a 5:1 ratio contains approximately 1.2 inches of liquid-water equivalent, while twelve inches of snow with a 20:1 ratio contains only 0.6 inches. Consequently, the shallower wet snow contains approximately twice as much water and weighs roughly twice as much per unit area as the deeper dry snow. How Heavy Snowstorms Develop​ Significant snowstorms generally require sufficient atmospheric moisture, cold temperatures, and a process that lifts air to produce precipitation. Several conditions can contribute to heavy snowfall: Atmospheric Moisture: Moisture provides the water vapor needed for ice crystal formation and growth. Rising Air: Weather systems and atmospheric disturbances lift air, allowing it to cool and produce clouds and precipitation. Favorable Temperatures: Cold atmospheric layers support the development and preservation of snowflakes. Orographic Lift: Mountains force approaching air upward, potentially enhancing snowfall along elevated terrain. Persistent Storm Systems: Slow-moving storms or repeated periods of snowfall can produce large accumulations. Snow Bands: Narrow areas of enhanced atmospheric lift can produce particularly intense snowfall rates over relatively small geographic areas. These conditions can cause large differences in snowfall accumulation between nearby locations. Understanding Snow Loads​ Snow accumulation places additional weight on roofs, canopies, and other structures. The weight of snow depends primarily on its water content rather than its depth alone. One inch of liquid water spread over one square foot weighs approximately 5.2 pounds. This means that snow containing one inch of liquid-water equivalent creates a load of approximately 5.2 pounds per square foot, before accounting for other factors. For example: Liquid-Water Equivalent Approximate Load 1 inch 5.2 lb/ft² 2 inches 10.4 lb/ft² 3 inches 15.6 lb/ft² 4 inches 20.8 lb/ft² Additional snowfall, rain absorbed by existing snow, and drifting can increase the weight placed on individual portions of a roof. Snow loads may also be distributed unevenly because of wind, roof shape, and surrounding structures. Actual structural risk depends on building design, roof geometry, local building requirements, and the distribution of accumulated snow. Learn More: National Weather Service — Winter Weather Additional Resource: National Weather Service — Understanding Snow-to-Liquid Ratios LikelihoodHighly Likely MagnitudeLimited Potential Impacts Health & Safety Utilities Transportation Communications Extreme Cold More Info Extreme cold occurs when temperatures fall significantly below normal for a particular region, creating hazardous conditions for people, animals, and infrastructure. Cold outbreaks often develop when large masses of Arctic or polar air move into lower latitudes. Strong winds can accelerate heat loss, making already cold conditions feel substantially colder. Provo experiences freezing temperatures throughout the winter, with occasional outbreaks of extreme cold. The surrounding Wasatch Mountains and Utah Valley influence local temperature patterns, particularly when cold air becomes trapped near the valley floor. Prolonged periods of subfreezing temperatures can affect developed neighborhoods, transportation corridors, and exposed infrastructure. Extreme cold can cause hypothermia, frostbite, and other cold-related injuries. Freezing temperatures can damage water pipes, affect vehicles and mechanical equipment, and increase demand for heating and electricity. Extended cold outbreaks may disrupt utilities, transportation, and essential services, particularly when accompanied by power outages or other winter-weather hazards. Local Example1924 — Provo Record Cold On December 27, 1924, Provo recorded a temperature of −30°F in historical weather records. About Extreme Cold × How Extreme Cold Develops​ Extreme cold often occurs when large masses of cold, dense air move southward from Arctic or polar regions. These air masses develop over areas where limited solar heating and prolonged winter darkness allow temperatures to fall significantly. Several atmospheric conditions contribute to extreme cold events: Arctic Air Masses: Large regions of very cold air form over northern latitudes and can spread southward into the United States. Jet Stream Patterns: Changes in the position and shape of the jet stream can allow cold polar air to move farther south than usual. High-Pressure Systems: Strong areas of high atmospheric pressure can produce clear skies, light winds, and conditions favorable for cooling. Radiational Cooling: At night, the Earth's surface releases heat through infrared radiation. Clear skies and light winds can allow temperatures near the ground to fall rapidly. Snow Cover: Snow reflects much of the Sun's incoming energy and can help maintain colder surface temperatures. Extreme cold can occur without substantial snowfall or strong winds. Understanding Wind Chill​ Wind chill describes how cold conditions feel to exposed human skin when wind increases the rate of heat loss. Under calm conditions, a thin layer of air warmed by the body forms near the skin's surface. Wind removes this relatively warm layer, allowing heat to escape more rapidly. The National Weather Service uses a wind chill index to estimate the combined effects of air temperature and wind speed. For example: Air Temperature Wind Speed Approximate Wind Chill 30°F 10 mph 21°F 20°F 15 mph 6°F 10°F 20 mph -9°F 0°F 15 mph -19°F -10°F 20 mph -35°F Wind chill does not represent a change in actual air temperature. Importantly, wind chill does not cause inanimate objects to become colder than the surrounding air. A water pipe exposed to 10°F air and a wind chill of -9°F can cool more quickly because of the wind, but it will not become colder than the actual 10°F air solely because of wind chill. Temperature Inversions and Cold-Air Pooling​ Under normal atmospheric conditions, air temperature generally decreases with increasing elevation. A temperature inversion occurs when a layer of warmer air sits above colder air near the surface. During clear, calm winter nights, the ground loses heat through radiation, cooling the air immediately above it. Because cold air is relatively dense, it can flow downhill and accumulate in valleys and other low-lying areas. This process is known as cold-air pooling. Several factors can help maintain a valley temperature inversion: Surrounding Mountains: Mountain terrain can restrict the horizontal movement of trapped cold air. Stable Atmospheric Conditions: High-pressure systems and weak winds can limit vertical mixing. Clear Nights: Strong radiational cooling lowers temperatures near the ground. Snow-Covered Ground: Snow cover can reinforce low surface temperatures by reflecting sunlight. These conditions can sometimes cause valley temperatures to be colder than temperatures at higher elevations. Utah Valley's geography makes temperature inversions and cold-air pooling particularly relevant to Provo. How Extreme Cold Affects the Human Body​ The human body maintains an internal temperature of approximately 98.6°F (37°C) through metabolic heat production and temperature regulation. When heat loss exceeds the body's ability to produce heat, body temperature begins to fall. Heat escapes through several processes: Radiation: The body emits heat toward cooler surroundings. Conduction: Heat transfers directly to colder surfaces through physical contact. Convection: Moving air or water carries heat away from the body. Evaporation: Moisture evaporating from the skin removes heat. Prolonged or severe cold exposure can produce two major medical conditions: Hypothermia: Occurs when core body temperature falls below 95°F (35°C). It can impair coordination, judgment, and normal bodily functions and may become fatal. Frostbite: Occurs when skin and underlying tissues freeze, potentially damaging cells and blood vessels. Fingers, toes, ears, and the nose are particularly vulnerable. The risk depends on temperature, wind, moisture, clothing, exposure duration, and individual circumstances. How Freezing Temperatures Affect Infrastructure​ Extreme cold can affect buildings, utilities, transportation systems, and mechanical equipment. Several physical processes contribute to cold-weather damage: Water Expansion: Water expands by approximately 9% when it freezes. Ice formation inside confined plumbing can create pressures capable of rupturing pipes and fittings. Thermal Contraction: Many materials contract as temperatures decrease. Temperature changes can place stress on joints, seals, and structural components. Reduced Battery Performance: Cold temperatures slow electrochemical reactions, reducing the available power and starting capability of some batteries. Changes in Material Properties: Some materials become more brittle or less flexible at very low temperatures. Increased Energy Demand: Heating systems require more energy as the difference between indoor and outdoor temperatures increases. Water pipes are particularly vulnerable when located in unheated spaces or exposed to prolonged freezing conditions. Pipe failure may not become apparent until temperatures rise and accumulated ice melts, allowing water to escape through damaged sections.
