About Train Derailment × How Trains Stay on the Tracks​ Railroad vehicles use specially designed steel wheels that travel along steel rails. Unlike automobile wheels, railroad wheels are shaped to guide the vehicle along a fixed path. Several design features help keep trains on the tracks: Wheel Tread: The portion of the wheel that normally contacts the rail. Railroad wheel treads are slightly tapered, helping wheelsets remain aligned with the track. Wheel Flange: A raised rim along the inner edge of the wheel. Flanges help prevent excessive sideways movement and provide guidance when necessary. Axles: Railroad wheels are typically connected by solid axles that keep each wheelset aligned and rotating together. Rails: Steel rails support the weight of the train and guide its movement. Cross Ties: Ties hold the rails in position and help maintain proper spacing. Ballast: Crushed stone beneath and around the ties distributes loads, provides drainage, and helps maintain track stability. The distance between the rails is known as the track gauge. Standard-gauge railroads in the United States use a gauge of 4 feet, 8.5 inches. Proper wheel geometry, track alignment, and rail condition are essential for maintaining stable train movement. How Train Derailments Occur​ A derailment happens when the forces acting on a railroad vehicle cause its wheels to leave their intended position on the rails. Several factors can contribute to derailments: Track Defects Track defects can interfere with the ability of wheels to remain properly supported and guided. Examples include: Broken or damaged rails. Improper track alignment. Excessive rail spacing. Defective switches. Unstable track foundations. Deteriorated ties or ballast. Mechanical Failures Railroad vehicles contain numerous mechanical components that must function correctly. Failures involving wheels, axles, bearings, suspension, or braking equipment can contribute to derailments. Excessive Speed Trains must operate within speed limits appropriate for track conditions, curvature, and other operating factors. Excessive speed through a curve can create lateral forces that exceed the track and vehicle's ability to maintain stable movement. Human Factors Errors involving train handling, switching, communications, or operating procedures can contribute to accidents. Environmental Conditions Flooding, severe weather, debris on the tracks, and ground movement can damage railroad infrastructure or interfere with operations. Derailments frequently involve multiple contributing factors rather than a single isolated failure. Types of Railroad Accidents​ Railroad accidents can take several different forms. Derailments: Occur when one or more railroad wheels leave the rails. Train Collisions: Occur when trains collide with other trains, railroad equipment, or obstructions. Grade-Crossing Accidents: Involve collisions between trains and vehicles or pedestrians at locations where roads or pathways cross railroad tracks. Switching Accidents: Occur during operations involving the movement, coupling, or positioning of railcars. Railroad Equipment Failures: Mechanical or structural problems may cause accidents even when a derailment does not occur. These categories can overlap. For example, a collision at a grade crossing may also cause several railcars to derail. Understanding Railroad Safety Systems​ Railroads use multiple technologies and procedures to reduce accident risks. Important systems include: Track Inspections Railroad tracks are inspected to identify conditions that could affect safe operations. Inspections may identify: Rail defects. Improper track geometry. Deteriorated ties. Damaged switches. Track foundation problems. Some inspections use specialized vehicles and electronic equipment to evaluate rail conditions. Hotbox Detectors Railroad wheel bearings can generate excessive heat when they begin to fail. Trackside hotbox detectors use infrared sensors to identify unusually hot bearings as trains pass. A detector may alert railroad personnel when temperatures exceed established thresholds. Bearing failures can be particularly dangerous because they may damage axles or other components and contribute to derailments. Dragging Equipment Detectors Trackside sensors can identify certain objects hanging beneath railcars that may strike or damage railroad infrastructure. Railroad Signaling Railroad signals communicate operating information and help control train movement. Depending on the system, signals can indicate whether a train may proceed, must slow down, or must stop. Positive Train Control (PTC) Positive Train Control is a technology designed to automatically intervene in certain unsafe operating situations. PTC is intended to help prevent: Train-to-train collisions. Derailments caused by excessive speed. Unauthorized movement into established work zones. Movement through switches left in the wrong position. PTC does not prevent every type of railroad accident. For example, it generally does not directly prevent derailments caused by broken rails or failed wheel bearings. Freight Trains and Hazardous Materials​ Freight railroads transport a wide variety of cargo, including: Consumer goods. Agricultural products. Construction materials. Fuels and petroleum products. Industrial chemicals. Manufactured equipment. Some freight trains carry materials classified as hazardous under federal transportation regulations. In a derailment, damaged railcars or containers may release their contents. The consequences depend on the type of cargo, the quantity involved, and the circumstances of the accident. In February 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed in East Palestine, Ohio. The accident involved hazardous material releases and became the subject of extensive federal investigations. Investigators determined that the derailment began with the failure of an overheated wheel bearing. This illustrates how a mechanical failure can contribute to a much larger transportation emergency. For additional information about chemical properties, exposure pathways, and hazardous substance identification, see the Hazardous Materials section of this page. Railroad Accidents in Provo​ Provo is located along a major regional railroad corridor. The Union Pacific rail network supports freight transportation through Utah Valley and connects the region to broader national rail networks. Railroad infrastructure also intersects or parallels portions of Provo's transportation system. A significant derailment could affect the surrounding community in several ways: Blocked Crossings: Derailed equipment may obstruct roads or prevent access across railroad tracks. Infrastructure Damage: Railcars and locomotives can damage tracks, signals, utilities, and nearby structures. Transportation Disruption: Rail operations and affected roadways may remain closed while the accident is investigated and cleared. Emergency Access: Blocked crossings can complicate movement between neighborhoods and delay emergency vehicles. Secondary Hazards: Fires, fuel spills, or hazardous material releases may create additional complications. The 2022 Pre-Disaster Mitigation Plan identifies Provo's railroad corridor as an important factor in transportation and emergency access planning. Because major transportation corridors and railroad crossings influence movement through the city, disruptions can affect areas beyond the immediate accident scene. They can include fires, explosions, mechanical failures, structural collapses, and uncontrolled chemical reactions. These incidents may result from equipment malfunctions, human error, environmental conditions, or failures of safety systems. Provo contains industrial, commercial, and utility facilities that depend on mechanical equipment, electrical systems, and complex operating processes. Facilities such as manufacturing plants, warehouses, processing operations, and utility installations can present different types of industrial hazards. The potential consequences depend on the materials, equipment, and activities involved at each location. Industrial accidents can cause serious injuries, fatalities, fires, explosions, and damage to buildings or nearby infrastructure. Significant incidents may disrupt electricity, water, transportation, or commercial operations and require specialized emergency response resources. In some cases, an initial equipment failure can trigger additional failures that increase the overall severity of the incident. Regional Example2025 — American Fork Chemical Explosion On March 19, 2025, a chemical explosion at a storage facility in nearby American Fork injured two people and prompted a regional hazardous materials response. About Industrial Accident × Types of Industrial Accidents​ Industrial facilities use machinery, energy systems, chemicals, and structural equipment to perform a wide range of operations. Accidents can occur when these systems fail or operate outside their intended conditions. Common types of industrial accidents include: Industrial Fires: Uncontrolled combustion involving equipment, combustible materials, fuels, or industrial processes. Explosions: Rapid releases of energy that produce pressure waves, heat, and potentially flying debris. Mechanical Failures: Malfunctions involving motors, pumps, turbines, conveyors, or other machinery. Pressure System Failures: Ruptures involving boilers, compressed-gas systems, pressure vessels, or industrial piping. Structural Failures: The partial or complete collapse of buildings, storage systems, platforms, or supporting structures. Chemical Process Accidents: Uncontrolled reactions or process failures that may release heat, pressure, or hazardous substances. Electrical Accidents: Equipment failures involving short circuits, electrical arcs, overheating, or other electrical hazards. Different accident types can occur together or trigger one another. How Industrial Accidents Occur​ Industrial facilities typically operate within established limits for temperature, pressure, speed, electrical load, and other conditions. Accidents can develop when equipment or processes move beyond these safe operating limits. Several factors may contribute: Equipment Deterioration: Corrosion, fatigue, wear, and aging can gradually weaken machinery and structural components. Mechanical Malfunctions: Bearings, valves, pumps, and other components can fail during operation. Human Factors: Miscommunication, incorrect procedures, insufficient training, or operational mistakes may contribute to unsafe conditions. Maintenance Problems: Undetected defects or inadequate maintenance can allow equipment problems to develop over time. Process Control Failures: Malfunctioning sensors, control systems, or automation equipment may fail to maintain safe operating conditions. External Events: Severe weather, earthquakes, utility failures, or other disasters can damage industrial facilities. Major industrial accidents often result from several contributing factors rather than a single isolated failure. Understanding Industrial Fires and Explosions​ Industrial fires and explosions can occur when combustible materials interact with ignition sources under suitable conditions. Industrial Fires Combustion requires three essential elements: Fuel. Heat. Oxygen or another oxidizing agent. These elements are commonly represented by the Fire Triangle. Industrial environments may contain additional hazards because fuels can exist as gases, vapors, liquids, dust, or solid materials. Some industrial fires can spread rapidly when combustible materials are concentrated or ventilation conditions are favorable. Industrial Explosions An explosion involves a rapid release of energy that produces a sudden increase in pressure. Several types of explosions can occur in industrial environments: Chemical Explosions: Rapid chemical reactions release energy, often producing heat and pressure. Physical Explosions: Stored pressure or other physical energy is released suddenly, such as when a pressurized vessel ruptures. Dust Explosions: Suspended combustible dust ignites within a confined or partially confined space. Vapor Cloud Explosions: A cloud of flammable vapor ignites under conditions that allow damaging pressure to develop. Two important combustion terms describe different flame behaviors: Deflagration: Combustion that propagates through a material at a speed below the local speed of sound. Detonation: A combustion process involving a shock wave that travels through the reactive material at supersonic speed. Both processes can produce destructive consequences, depending on the materials and surrounding conditions. Understanding Industrial Equipment Failures​ Industrial operations frequently rely on equipment containing substantial amounts of stored energy. This energy may be mechanical, electrical, thermal, or stored within pressurized systems. Pressure Vessels Pressure vessels are containers designed to hold gases or liquids at pressures different from the surrounding atmosphere. Examples include: Compressed-air tanks. Boilers. Industrial reactors. Pressurized storage vessels. Refrigeration equipment. A pressure vessel can fail if internal pressure exceeds its structural capacity or if the vessel becomes weakened by deterioration or damage. A sudden rupture can release stored energy, producing a powerful pressure wave and potentially projecting fragments of the vessel. Mechanical Equipment Industrial machinery often contains moving parts operating at high speeds or under substantial loads. Failures involving rotating machinery, bearings, shafts, or other components can damage surrounding equipment and create additional hazards. Electrical Systems Electrical equipment can fail through insulation breakdown, short circuits, overheating, or other faults. Some electrical failures produce an arc flash, which is a sudden release of energy through an electrical arc. Arc flashes can generate intense heat, bright light, and pressure effects. How Industrial Accidents Escalate​ Industrial accidents sometimes develop into larger emergencies through a sequence of connected failures. This process is often described as a cascading failure. For example: Initial Equipment Failure: A mechanical component fails during normal operation. Loss of Process Control: The failure causes operating conditions to move outside their intended limits. Safety System Failure: An automatic shutdown or protective device fails to respond as intended. Secondary Damage: Increasing pressure, temperature, or mechanical stress damages additional equipment. Major Incident: The combined failures result in a fire, explosion, or other serious accident. This is an illustrative sequence. Actual accidents can develop through many different pathways. Industrial safety engineering frequently uses multiple independent protective measures to reduce the likelihood of such escalation. Understanding Industrial Safety Systems​ Industrial facilities use a variety of engineered systems and operating practices to control hazards. Common protective systems include: Process Monitoring: Sensors measure temperatures, pressures, flow rates, and other operating conditions. Automatic Shutdown Systems: Equipment can be stopped when unsafe conditions are detected. Pressure Relief Devices: Safety valves and other devices help protect systems against excessive pressure. Fire Detection Systems: Sensors identify heat, smoke, or flames. Fire Suppression Systems: Specialized systems may control or extinguish fires involving industrial equipment and materials. Secondary Containment: Barriers and containment structures can limit the spread of certain spilled materials. Redundant Safety Systems: Multiple independent protective systems reduce dependence on any single component. These protective measures are often referred to as layers of protection. The purpose is to reduce the likelihood that an individual equipment failure will develop into a catastrophic accident. Understanding Process Safety Management​ Process Safety Management (PSM) is a systematic approach to identifying and controlling hazards associated with certain industrial processes. OSHA regulates process safety management for covered operations involving highly hazardous chemicals. Important elements of PSM include: Identifying process hazards. Maintaining equipment integrity. Establishing operating procedures. Training personnel. Managing changes to equipment and operating processes. Investigating incidents. Evaluating emergency procedures. The Environmental Protection Agency also administers the Risk Management Program (RMP), which applies to certain facilities handling specified hazardous substances above regulatory threshold quantities. Covered facilities must evaluate potential accidental releases, maintain prevention programs, and address emergency response. These regulations are intended to reduce the likelihood and consequences of serious industrial chemical accidents. Industrial Accidents in Provo​ Provo contains a variety of commercial, industrial, and utility facilities that support the community. These operations may involve: Manufacturing equipment. Electrical distribution systems. Heating and cooling systems. Warehousing and material handling. Water and wastewater infrastructure. Mechanical and processing equipment. Different facilities present different hazards depending on their activities, materials, and equipment. A significant industrial accident could affect surrounding neighborhoods and infrastructure even when the incident remains confined to a single facility. For example, damage to an essential utility installation could interrupt services for customers located far from the original incident. The 2022 Pre-Disaster Mitigation Plan recognizes industrial and technological hazards as part of regional emergency planning. However, it does not provide a separate likelihood and magnitude assessment for industrial accidents in Provo. Interruptions can result from equipment failures, damaged power lines, severe weather, accidents, or disturbances affecting the larger electrical grid. Outages may affect individual buildings, entire neighborhoods, or large geographic regions. Provo operates its own municipal electric utility, Provo Power, which maintains electrical distribution infrastructure throughout the city. The system depends on substations, transformers, power lines, and connections to regional electricity resources. Damage to this infrastructure or disruptions to the broader electrical network can interrupt service to Provo residents and businesses. Power outages can disrupt heating, cooling, lighting, communications, traffic signals, businesses, and other essential services. Extended outages may also affect medical equipment, water and wastewater infrastructure, refrigeration, and emergency response operations. Widespread electrical failures can create cascading disruptions as other critical systems lose power. Local Example2026 — Provo Power Outage In September 2026, a third-party outage tracker reported approximately 405 customers without electricity in Provo. About Power Outage × How the Electrical Grid Works​ The electrical grid is an interconnected network that generates, transmits, and distributes electricity to consumers. The system is commonly divided into three major components: 1. Electricity Generation Electricity is produced at generating facilities using sources such as: Natural gas. Coal. Hydroelectric power. Nuclear energy. Solar energy. Wind energy. Generators convert mechanical or other forms of energy into electrical energy. 2. Electrical Transmission Electricity is transported over long distances using high-voltage transmission lines. Higher transmission voltages allow large amounts of electrical power to be transported while reducing resistive losses. Substations and transformers connect different portions of the grid and change voltage levels. 3. Electrical Distribution Distribution systems deliver electricity from substations to homes, businesses, and other facilities. Distribution lines typically operate at lower voltages than major transmission lines. Transformers located throughout neighborhoods further reduce voltage to levels suitable for individual customers. A simplified electricity pathway is: Generating Facility → Transmission Lines → Substation → Distribution Lines → Transformer → Customer The electrical grid must continuously balance electricity generation with consumer demand. Significant imbalances or equipment problems can affect system stability and interrupt electrical service. What Causes Power Outages?​ Power outages can develop from many different causes. Common contributing factors include: Severe Weather: Strong winds, lightning, snow, and ice can damage power lines, poles, transformers, and other equipment. Equipment Failures: Transformers, switches, cables, and other electrical components can fail because of age, deterioration, or unexpected malfunctions. Vehicle Accidents: Vehicles striking utility poles or electrical equipment can interrupt service. Vegetation Contact: Trees and branches contacting electrical lines can cause faults or damage. Wildlife: Animals contacting energized equipment can cause electrical faults. Construction Damage: Excavation or other construction activity can damage underground electrical cables. Grid Disturbances: Problems affecting generation, transmission, or regional grid stability can interrupt power across larger areas. Planned Maintenance: Utilities sometimes disconnect equipment intentionally to perform repairs, inspections, or system improvements. The extent of an outage depends on which electrical components are affected and how the system is configured. Types of Power Outages​ Not all electrical interruptions occur in the same way. Several terms describe different types of power disturbances: Localized Outage An interruption affecting a limited area, such as a building, street, or neighborhood. Localized outages often result from problems involving distribution equipment. Widespread Blackout A loss of electrical service affecting a large geographic area or substantial number of customers. Large blackouts may involve transmission failures, generation problems, or cascading grid disturbances. Brownout A reduction in electrical voltage below its normal operating level. A brownout does not necessarily involve a complete loss of electricity, but reduced voltage can affect the operation of equipment. Momentary Interruption A brief loss of electrical service, sometimes lasting only a fraction of a second or several seconds. These interruptions may occur when protective equipment temporarily disconnects a circuit and then restores service. Rolling Blackout An intentional interruption of electrical service to selected areas for limited periods. Rolling blackouts may be used as an emergency measure to reduce electrical demand when sufficient supply is unavailable. How Electrical Failures Spread​ Electrical systems contain protective devices designed to identify faults and disconnect affected equipment. These systems help prevent a localized failure from damaging additional infrastructure. Important protective devices include: Circuit Breakers: Disconnect electrical circuits when abnormal conditions are detected. Fuses: Interrupt electrical current when excessive current causes the protective element to melt. Protective Relays: Monitor electrical conditions and signal circuit breakers when certain faults occur. Reclosers: Automatically interrupt and attempt to restore electrical service following certain distribution faults. Sectionalizing Equipment: Helps isolate damaged portions of a distribution network. Under normal conditions, these devices reduce the extent of outages. However, a disturbance affecting one part of an interconnected grid can sometimes place additional stress on other components. Understanding Cascading Blackouts​ A cascading blackout occurs when an initial electrical disturbance triggers additional failures across the power system. For example: Initial Failure: A major transmission line becomes unavailable. Power Redistribution: Electricity flows through other available transmission paths. Additional Overloading: Some remaining lines may exceed their safe operating limits. Protective Disconnection: Protective systems disconnect overloaded or unstable equipment. Cascading Failures: Additional disconnections may further destabilize the network. If the disturbance continues, large portions of the electrical grid may lose power. This is why electrical grid operators continuously monitor power flows, frequency, voltage, and system stability. Not every major equipment failure causes a cascading blackout. Grid design and protective systems are intended to limit these consequences. How Power Is Restored​ Restoring electrical service depends on the location and cause of the outage. Utility operators generally work through several stages: 1. Identifying the Problem Monitoring systems, protective equipment, and field reports help determine which portions of the system are affected. 2. Isolating Damaged Equipment Faulted lines, transformers, or other components are disconnected so unaffected portions of the grid can potentially be restored safely. 3. Reconfiguring the System Utilities may use switching operations to restore electricity through alternate available paths. 4. Repairing Infrastructure Crews replace or repair damaged lines, poles, transformers, and other electrical equipment. 5. Restoring Service Electrical circuits are reenergized after required safety checks and repairs. Restoration may occur in stages rather than simultaneously for all affected customers. Black Start Following certain major regional blackouts, some generating facilities may need to restart without receiving electricity from the external grid. This process is called black start. Specialized generating resources can provide initial power so additional generating facilities and transmission systems can be brought online. Black-start procedures are primarily relevant to major grid restoration, rather than ordinary neighborhood outages. Understanding Electrical Grid Frequency​ In the United States, most interconnected alternating-current electrical systems operate at 60 Hz. This means the electrical current completes 60 cycles each second. Maintaining stable grid frequency requires balancing electrical generation and demand. Insufficient Generation: When electrical demand exceeds available generation, system frequency tends to decrease. Excess Generation: When generation exceeds demand, frequency tends to increase. Significant frequency deviations can threaten grid stability. Automated protective systems may disconnect loads or generating facilities to prevent more serious system disturbances. Grid frequency is therefore an important indicator of the balance between electricity supply and demand. Power Outages in Provo​ Provo operates its own municipally owned electric utility, known as Provo Power. Provo Power maintains the city's electrical distribution infrastructure, including: Power lines. Utility poles. Distribution transformers. Substations. Electrical switching equipment. System monitoring infrastructure. Provo Power is a member of the Utah Municipal Power Agency (UMPA), which coordinates electrical resources for Provo and several other municipal utilities. The city's electric infrastructure is connected to broader regional electrical resources. Consequently, outages may originate from problems within Provo's distribution system or from disturbances affecting the larger electrical network. Electrical System Monitoring Provo Power maintains a 24-hour electrical dispatch operation and uses an Outage Management System (OMS) to identify and monitor electrical interruptions. Its official website also provides information about current and recent outages. Why Power Outages Matter for Emergency Communications PACT relies on electrical and communications infrastructure to support emergency operations. Electrical outages can affect: Amateur radio repeaters without functioning backup power. Internet connections and network equipment. Cellular towers and associated infrastructure. Radio charging equipment. Emergency Operations Center systems. Other communications equipment dependent on external electricity. The degree of disruption depends on available backup power, equipment configuration, and the duration of the outage. About Acts of Violence × Types of Violent Emergencies​ Violent emergencies can include active assailant incidents, mass violence, targeted attacks, terrorism, and attacks against critical infrastructure. These categories may overlap, but not all violent crimes constitute terrorism or large-scale emergencies. Terrorism is distinguished by specific motivations and objectives, while targeted violence may arise from personal grievances or other circumstances. Mass Casualty Incidents​ A Mass Casualty Incident (MCI) occurs when the number or severity of casualties exceeds the resources immediately available to respond effectively. MCIs can result from violent attacks, transportation accidents, natural disasters, and other emergencies. Emergency medical personnel may use triage systems to prioritize treatment and transportation according to patient needs and available resources. Community Impacts​ Significant acts of violence can affect communities beyond the immediate incident location. Potential consequences include: Injuries, fatalities, and increased demand for emergency medical services. Evacuations, restricted access, and transportation disruptions. Damage to buildings and essential infrastructure. Interruptions to electricity, water, or communications services. Long-term psychological, economic, and community recovery needs. Attacks against critical infrastructure can have particularly widespread consequences by disrupting essential services. Emergency Response Coordination​ Serious violent incidents may require coordinated operations involving law enforcement, fire departments, emergency medical services, and emergency management agencies. Responders may use the Incident Command System (ICS) to organize personnel, resources, communications, and incident objectives. When multiple agencies share responsibilities, a Unified Command structure may be established. Emergency management agencies may activate an Emergency Operations Center (EOC) to support resource coordination, situational awareness, and public information. Acts of Violence in Provo​ Provo contains educational institutions, residential neighborhoods, commercial districts, public facilities, and major transportation corridors. A significant violent incident could require a coordinated response involving Provo Police, Provo Fire & Rescue, emergency medical providers, Utah County agencies, and Provo City Emergency Management. Large-scale incidents may increase demand on emergency communications systems or cause localized service disruptions. When activated, PACT may support authorized emergency management operations by maintaining communications and assisting with information flow. PACT members operate under the direction of emergency management and do not perform law enforcement or security functions. Significant incidents can create widespread operational disruptions and require extended recovery efforts. Local Example2026 — NewspaperArchive Cyberattack In February 2026, NewspaperArchive, a Provo-associated online archive service, reported a cyberattack that disrupted access to its systems. About Cyber Attack × Types of Cyber Attacks​ Cyberattacks use different techniques to compromise computer systems, steal information, or disrupt operations. Common types include: Malware: Malicious software designed to damage systems, steal information, or disrupt operations. Ransomware: Malware that blocks access to files or systems, often accompanied by demands for payment. Phishing: Fraudulent messages or websites intended to steal information or trick users into unsafe actions. Denial-of-Service (DoS): Attacks that overwhelm or disrupt systems, preventing legitimate access. Distributed attacks (DDoS) involve multiple devices. Credential Attacks: Attempts to steal or misuse passwords, accounts, or other authentication information. Supply Chain Attacks: Compromises involving software, equipment, or services provided by third parties. A single cyberattack may involve several of these techniques. How Cyber Attacks Occur​ Cyberattacks often exploit weaknesses in technology, security practices, or human behavior. Common vulnerabilities include: Software Vulnerabilities: Security flaws that allow unauthorized access or actions. Compromised Credentials: Stolen passwords or authentication information. Social Engineering: Manipulating individuals into disclosing information or performing unauthorized actions. Misconfigured Systems: Incorrect security settings that expose networks or information. Third-Party Dependencies: Security incidents affecting external technology providers. Insider Threats: Intentional or accidental security incidents involving authorized users. Attackers may exploit multiple weaknesses during a single incident. Understanding Ransomware​ Ransomware can prevent organizations from accessing essential files, applications, or computer systems. Attackers typically demand payment to restore access and may also threaten to release stolen information. Consequences can include: Loss of access to important data and systems. Disruption of essential operations. Exposure of sensitive information. Financial losses and recovery expenses. Extended interruptions while systems are restored. Some incidents involve double extortion, in which attackers both encrypt data and threaten to publish stolen information. Paying a ransom does not guarantee that systems will be restored or stolen information will remain private. Understanding the CIA Triad​ Cybersecurity is commonly organized around three principles known as the CIA Triad: Principle Meaning Confidentiality Protecting information from unauthorized access. Integrity Ensuring information remains accurate and trustworthy. Availability Keeping systems and information accessible when needed. Cyberattacks may compromise one or more of these principles, potentially exposing sensitive information, altering records, or disrupting essential services. Cyber Attacks Against Critical Infrastructure​ Critical infrastructure increasingly relies on computer systems and communications networks to operate essential services. Potentially affected sectors include: Electricity and natural gas. Water and wastewater. Transportation. Healthcare. Communications. Financial and government services. Emergency services. Two important categories of technology include: Information Technology (IT): Systems used for data processing, communications, records, and business operations. Operational Technology (OT): Systems used to monitor or control physical equipment, such as electrical infrastructure and water treatment facilities. Some OT environments use Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems to monitor and control infrastructure. Cyberattacks against these systems can disrupt essential services and potentially affect physical operations. How Cyber Incidents Can Spread​ Organizations often depend on interconnected computer networks, cloud platforms, and third-party service providers. A cyberattack affecting one system may disrupt other connected services or organizations. For example, a compromised service provider could interrupt operations for multiple customers that depend on its technology. Recovery may require coordination among affected organizations, technology providers, and emergency management agencies. Cybersecurity and Emergency Communications​ Emergency communications systems have different technological dependencies, which can influence their vulnerability to cyberattacks. Internet-Dependent Communications Email, internet messaging, cloud applications, Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP), and internet-linked radio systems may be disrupted when underlying networks or service providers are compromised. Radio Communications Conventional VHF and UHF simplex radio communications can operate independently of the internet. Standalone repeaters may also continue functioning if their power and equipment remain operational. However, radio systems that depend on network links, centralized controllers, or internet services may experience disruptions when those supporting systems are affected. Satellite Communications Satellite services depend on ground stations, computer networks, and supporting infrastructure that may also be vulnerable to cyber incidents. Emergency Coordination Systems Cyberattacks can disrupt software used for dispatch, resource coordination, situational awareness, and emergency information sharing, even when physical communications infrastructure remains functional. Cyber Attacks in Provo​ Provo relies on interconnected technology to support municipal operations, electrical and water utilities, transportation, healthcare, educational institutions, emergency services, and local businesses. A significant cyberattack could disrupt essential services, interfere with government operations, or complicate emergency response activities. The 2022 Pre-Disaster Mitigation Plan emphasizes infrastructure protection and continuity of essential services but does not provide a separate cyberattack likelihood or magnitude assessment for Provo. Contaminants may originate from natural geological processes, agricultural and industrial activities, sewage, or damaged infrastructure. Depending on the substance involved, contaminated water may become unsafe for drinking, cooking, or other uses. Provo relies primarily on springs and groundwater wells, along with treated surface water from regional sources. These supplies can be vulnerable to different forms of contamination depending on surrounding land use, geological conditions, and infrastructure integrity. Protecting water sources and maintaining reliable treatment and distribution systems are important components of the city's water infrastructure. Water contamination can cause illness, expose residents to harmful chemicals, and interrupt access to safe drinking water. Significant incidents may require public water advisories, additional treatment, or temporary restrictions on water use. Contamination affecting major water infrastructure could disrupt homes, businesses, healthcare facilities, and other essential community services. Local Example2015 — Provo River Oil Spill On November 28, 2015, a tanker overturned in Provo Canyon, releasing approximately 4,500 gallons of crude oil. Some entered the Provo River, and officials temporarily closed a downstream drinking-water intake. About Water Contamination × Types of Water Contamination​ Water can become contaminated by several different categories of substances. The nature of the contaminant determines its potential effects and the methods required to remove or control it. Biological Contamination Biological contamination involves microorganisms capable of causing disease. Common examples include: Bacteria: Organisms such as certain strains of E. coli, Salmonella, and Campylobacter. Viruses: Disease-causing viruses such as norovirus and hepatitis A. Protozoa: Microscopic parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium. Biological contamination may result from sewage, animal waste, or other sources of disease-causing organisms. Chemical Contamination Chemical contaminants may occur naturally or enter water through human activities. Examples include: Arsenic and other naturally occurring elements. Lead and copper from certain plumbing materials. Nitrates associated with fertilizers and waste. Pesticides and agricultural chemicals. Petroleum products and industrial solvents. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Chemical contaminants vary considerably in their toxicity and environmental behavior. Some produce immediate health effects, while others may cause harm following repeated or prolonged exposure. Radiological Contamination Radiological contamination occurs when radioactive substances are present in water. Certain radioactive elements occur naturally in rocks and groundwater. Examples include: Uranium. Radium. Radon. The potential health effects depend on the radioactive material, its concentration, and the duration of exposure. Physical Contamination Physical contaminants affect the appearance or physical characteristics of water. Examples include: Sediment. Suspended soil particles. Organic debris. Other particulate materials. Physical changes do not always mean water is unsafe, but they can indicate changes in water quality or interfere with treatment. How Drinking Water Becomes Contaminated​ Drinking water can become contaminated at several points between its original source and the consumer. Source Water Contamination Contaminants may enter groundwater, rivers, reservoirs, or other drinking water sources. Potential sources include: Agricultural runoff. Industrial discharges. Leaking underground storage tanks. Sewage or wastewater releases. Naturally occurring minerals. Stormwater carrying pollutants. Treatment System Problems Water treatment facilities use processes designed to control or remove contaminants. Equipment failures, operational problems, or water-quality changes can reduce treatment effectiveness. Distribution System Contamination Water may also become contaminated after leaving a treatment facility. Distribution systems contain pipes, valves, pumps, and storage facilities. Potential causes include: Broken or damaged water mains. Loss of water pressure. Cross-connections with unsafe water. Improperly protected storage facilities. Deteriorated plumbing materials. A contamination incident may affect an individual building, a portion of a distribution network, or an entire water supply system. Surface Water vs. Groundwater​ Drinking water generally comes from two broad categories of natural sources. Surface Water Surface water includes: Rivers. Streams. Lakes. Reservoirs. These sources are directly exposed to surrounding environmental conditions. Rainfall, runoff, wildlife, and human activities can introduce microorganisms, sediment, or chemicals. Surface water typically requires filtration and disinfection before distribution as public drinking water. Groundwater Groundwater is water stored underground within soil, sediment, and rock formations. These underground water-bearing formations are known as aquifers. Groundwater may be accessed through wells or emerge naturally at springs. As water moves through underground materials, some contaminants can be filtered or reduced. However, groundwater is not automatically free of contamination. Dissolved minerals, agricultural chemicals, industrial pollutants, and microorganisms can sometimes reach underground water supplies. Groundwater contamination can be particularly challenging because some pollutants move slowly and may remain underground for extended periods. How Drinking Water Is Treated​ Public drinking water systems use treatment processes appropriate for their water sources and identified contaminants. Common treatment processes include: Coagulation and Flocculation Treatment chemicals may be added to help small suspended particles combine into larger particles. These larger particles are easier to remove. Sedimentation Water is allowed to move slowly through a basin, allowing heavier particles to settle. Filtration Water passes through filter media or other treatment systems designed to remove suspended particles and certain contaminants. Disinfection Disinfection reduces or inactivates disease-causing microorganisms. Common disinfection methods include: Chlorine-based disinfectants. Ultraviolet light. Ozone. Different methods have different advantages and limitations. Specialized Treatment Some contaminants require additional treatment technologies. Examples include: Activated carbon adsorption. Ion exchange. Reverse osmosis. Specialized filtration processes. Not every drinking water facility uses all of these treatment methods. The required treatment depends on the source water, contaminant characteristics, and applicable regulations. Understanding Water Quality Monitoring​ Public drinking water systems are required to monitor water quality according to applicable regulations. Testing may evaluate: Microorganisms. Chemical contaminants. Disinfectant levels. Turbidity. Other regulated water-quality indicators. Turbidity measures the cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles. Elevated turbidity can interfere with certain treatment processes and may indicate changing source-water conditions. Maximum Contaminant Levels The Environmental Protection Agency establishes enforceable drinking water standards for many regulated contaminants. A Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) is the highest permitted concentration of a regulated contaminant in drinking water, subject to applicable regulatory requirements. Some contaminants are regulated through treatment techniques rather than numerical MCLs. Public water systems must provide annual water-quality information through Consumer Confidence Reports. Understanding Drinking Water Advisories​ When drinking water may be unsafe, public water systems and health authorities may issue an advisory. Three major advisory categories are commonly used. Advisory Meaning Boil Water Water may contain harmful microorganisms; boiling according to official instructions can make it microbiologically safer Do Not Drink Water must not be consumed or used for food and beverage preparation Do Not Use Water must not be used for any purpose covered by the advisory because exposure may be dangerous Boil Water Advisory A Boil Water Advisory is generally issued when microbial contamination is suspected or confirmed. Boiling can inactivate many disease-causing bacteria, viruses, and parasites. However, boiling does not reliably remove hazardous chemicals, heavy metals, or radioactive contaminants. Do Not Drink Advisory A Do Not Drink Advisory may be issued when consuming the water presents a risk that cannot be addressed through boiling. Other uses, such as bathing or washing, may also be restricted, depending on the contaminant. Do Not Use Advisory A Do Not Use Advisory indicates that water should not be used for purposes identified in the official notice. Such advisories may involve contaminants capable of causing harm through contact, inhalation, or other exposure routes. The specific instructions provided by the water utility or public health authority always take precedence over general advisory descriptions. Why Water Pressure Matters​ Municipal water distribution systems normally maintain positive internal pressure. This pressure helps move water through pipes and reduces the likelihood that surrounding groundwater or soil water will enter through small openings. A significant loss of pressure can increase contamination concerns, particularly when damaged pipes are exposed to contaminated surroundings. Pressure loss may occur because of: Major water main breaks. Pump or equipment failures. Storage system problems. Other distribution disruptions. Following certain pressure-loss incidents, a water utility may issue a precautionary Boil Water Advisory while evaluating water quality. However, a water main break does not automatically mean contamination occurred. Water Contamination in Provo​ Provo operates a municipal drinking water system that serves residents, businesses, and essential facilities. The city's culinary water supplies include: Springs: Natural groundwater sources that supply a substantial portion of Provo's water. Groundwater Wells: Wells that provide water from underground aquifers and supplement other available sources. Treated Surface Water: Water originating from regional surface sources, including the Provo River and Deer Creek system. Provo's water system also includes storage facilities, pumping equipment, treatment infrastructure, and distribution pipelines. Protecting Groundwater Because groundwater is an important part of Provo's water supply, protecting underground sources is particularly relevant to the city. Contaminants introduced at the ground surface can sometimes migrate through soil and rock into aquifers. The potential for migration depends on local geology, groundwater movement, and the characteristics of the contaminant. Protecting Distribution Infrastructure Water distribution systems must maintain adequate operating conditions to deliver safe water. Damage to critical pipes, storage facilities, or pumping systems can interrupt service and may require additional water-quality monitoring. Community-Wide Consequences A significant drinking water contamination incident could affect: Residential water use. Restaurants and food service. Schools and universities. Healthcare facilities. Commercial operations. Other essential services. The 2022 Pre-Disaster Mitigation Plan emphasizes the importance of water infrastructure and reliable water supplies. However, it does not assign a separate likelihood and magnitude rating for water contamination in Provo. Learn More: CDC — What Causes Tap Water Contamination Water Advisories: EPA — Drinking Water Advisory Types Drinking Water Standards: EPA — National Primary Drinking Water Regulations Local Resource: Provo City — Water and Sewer LikelihoodHigh MagnitudeCritical Potential Impacts Health & Safety Air Quality Environment Economic Activity Poor Air Quality More Info Poor air quality occurs when airborne pollutants reach concentrations that may harm human health or the environment. Common pollutants include fine particulate matter, ground-level ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and carbon monoxide. These substances may be emitted directly into the atmosphere or form through chemical reactions involving other pollutants. Provo is located in Utah Valley, where surrounding mountains and seasonal weather patterns can contribute to pollution accumulation. During winter temperature inversions, cold air becomes trapped beneath warmer air, limiting atmospheric mixing and allowing fine particulate matter to build up. Wildfire smoke and summertime ozone formation can also reduce air quality throughout the region. Exposure to elevated air pollution can irritate the respiratory system, aggravate asthma, and increase the risk of cardiovascular and respiratory problems. Fine particles can penetrate deep into the lungs, while certain gaseous pollutants can inflame airways and reduce lung function. Severe or prolonged pollution episodes can affect public health, outdoor activities, and community operations. Local ExampleJanuary 2013 — Severe Provo Winter Inversion On January 22, 2013, a Provo air monitor recorded a 24-hour PM2.5 concentration of 124.5 micrograms per cubic meter during a winter inversion. About Poor Air Quality × Understanding Air Pollutants​ Air pollution consists of particles and gases that can affect human health, visibility, ecosystems, and the environment. The Environmental Protection Agency identifies six major categories of common outdoor air pollutants, known as criteria air pollutants. These include: Particulate matter. Ground-level ozone. Carbon monoxide. Sulfur dioxide. Nitrogen dioxide. Lead. Different pollutants originate from different sources and behave differently in the atmosphere. Particulate Matter (PM) Particulate matter consists of microscopic solid particles and liquid droplets suspended in the air. Two commonly measured categories are: PM2.5: Fine particles with aerodynamic diameters of 2.5 micrometers or smaller. PM10: Inhalable particles with aerodynamic diameters of 10 micrometers or smaller. For comparison, a human hair is typically tens of micrometers in diameter. PM2.5 particles are particularly concerning because they can penetrate deeply into the respiratory system. Some fine particles and their constituents can also enter the bloodstream. Sources of particulate pollution include: Vehicle emissions. Wood burning. Industrial operations. Construction and road dust. Wildfire smoke. Atmospheric chemical reactions. Not all particulate matter is emitted directly. A substantial portion of wintertime PM2.5 pollution in northern Utah forms through chemical reactions in the atmosphere. Ground-Level Ozone (O3) Ground-level ozone is a gas formed through chemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in the presence of sunlight. Ozone in the upper atmosphere protects Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation. However, ozone near the ground is an air pollutant that can damage lung tissue and aggravate respiratory conditions. Carbon Monoxide (CO) Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete combustion. Sources include motor vehicles, engines, and other fuel-burning equipment. Carbon monoxide reduces the blood's ability to transport oxygen. Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) Nitrogen dioxide is a reactive gas associated with combustion processes. It can contribute to respiratory irritation and participate in the formation of ozone and fine particles. Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) Sulfur dioxide is produced primarily when sulfur-containing fuels or materials are burned or processed. It can irritate the respiratory system and contribute to the formation of sulfate particles. Lead (Pb) Lead is a toxic metal that can enter the atmosphere through certain industrial processes and other sources. Airborne lead exposure can affect the nervous system and other organs. How Temperature Inversions Form​ Under typical atmospheric conditions, air temperature decreases as altitude increases through the lower atmosphere. Warmer air near the ground can rise and mix with cooler air above. This vertical mixing helps disperse pollutants. During a temperature inversion, warmer air is positioned above a layer of cooler air near the ground. The warmer layer suppresses vertical mixing, allowing pollutants to accumulate within the colder air. Several conditions favor winter inversions: Clear Skies: The ground loses heat rapidly during nighttime. Long Winter Nights: Extended cooling allows dense cold air to accumulate. Calm Winds: Weak winds limit atmospheric mixing. Snow Cover: Snow reflects sunlight and helps keep the ground and nearby air relatively cold. High Pressure Systems: Persistent atmospheric conditions can suppress mixing and maintain the inversion. Mountainous Terrain: Surrounding mountains can help contain cold air within valleys. Why Inversions Are Common in Utah Valley Utah Valley is bordered by the Wasatch Mountains to the east and other elevated terrain to the west and south. During winter, cold air can accumulate within the valley while warmer air remains above. The resulting inversion restricts the vertical movement of pollutants. Vehicle exhaust, residential heating, commercial activities, and other sources continue adding emissions to the trapped air. Over several days, pollutant concentrations may increase substantially. Inversions are not themselves pollutants. They are atmospheric conditions that can concentrate pollutants already present in the air. How Inversions End Inversions typically weaken when weather conditions restore atmospheric mixing. Strong winds, approaching storm systems, and changes in temperature can disrupt the stable air layers. Once mixing resumes, accumulated pollutants can disperse more effectively. Understanding Secondary Particulate Formation​ An important characteristic of Utah's winter pollution is that much of the PM2.5 is not emitted directly as particles. Instead, gases released from different sources react in the atmosphere and form new particles. These are called secondary particulates. Important precursor pollutants include: Nitrogen oxides (NOx). Ammonia (NH3). Volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Sulfur dioxide (SO2). Atmospheric reactions involving these substances can produce particulate compounds such as ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulfate. Ammonium nitrate is a major component of fine particulate pollution during northern Utah winter inversion episodes. This means that reducing directly emitted smoke or dust alone does not address every source of PM2.5. Gaseous precursor emissions can also contribute substantially to the development of poor air quality. How Wildfire Smoke Affects Air Quality​ Wildfires release a complex mixture of gases and airborne particles. The exact composition depends on the vegetation, materials being burned, combustion conditions, and atmospheric processes. Wildfire smoke commonly contains: Fine particulate matter. Carbon monoxide. Volatile organic compounds. Nitrogen oxides. Other combustion products. Long-Distance Smoke Transport Wildfire smoke can travel hundreds or thousands of miles from the original fire. Winds transport smoke through the atmosphere, sometimes carrying it across multiple states. Atmospheric conditions determine whether smoke remains elevated or mixes down toward the ground. Consequently, communities can experience unhealthy air quality even when no wildfire is burning nearby. Smoke and Visibility Smoke particles scatter and absorb sunlight, producing haze and reducing visibility. However, visibility alone is not a reliable measurement of health risk. Some harmful pollutants may be present even when the air does not appear visibly smoky. Wildfire Smoke vs. Winter Inversions Wildfire smoke introduces pollutants generated by combustion. Winter inversions primarily describe atmospheric conditions that restrict pollution dispersion. These are different phenomena, although smoke can accumulate during an inversion if both occur at the same time. How Ground-Level Ozone Forms​ Ground-level ozone is not usually emitted directly from vehicles or industrial equipment. Instead, it develops through chemical reactions involving precursor pollutants. Two important precursor groups include: Nitrogen Oxides (NOx): Emitted by vehicles, combustion equipment, and other sources. Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs): Released from fuels, solvents, vegetation, and various industrial and commercial activities. Sunlight drives reactions involving these substances that can produce ozone near the ground. Why Ozone Is Often a Summer Concern Ozone formation is generally favored by strong sunlight, warm temperatures, and suitable atmospheric conditions. As a result, elevated ozone concentrations commonly develop during warm, sunny weather. Ozone concentrations can vary throughout the day. They may increase during daylight hours as photochemical reactions become more active. The relationship between ozone and precursor emissions is complex. Changes in one precursor do not necessarily produce proportional changes in ozone levels. Understanding the Air Quality Index​ The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a standardized system developed by the Environmental Protection Agency to communicate outdoor air pollution levels and associated health concerns. The AQI uses a numerical scale divided into six major categories. AQI Category Color 0–50 Good Green 51–100 Moderate Yellow 101–150 Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups Orange 151–200 Unhealthy Red 201–300 Very Unhealthy Purple 301–500 Hazardous Maroon Higher AQI values indicate greater levels of health concern. How AQI Is Calculated Air-quality measurements are converted into pollutant-specific AQI values. The calculations use concentration breakpoints established for different pollutants and averaging periods. The reported overall AQI generally reflects the highest applicable pollutant-specific AQI. For example, PM2.5 may be the dominant pollutant during a winter inversion, while ozone may determine the AQI on a summer afternoon. AQI vs. Pollutant Concentration AQI is not itself a pollutant concentration. Pollutants are measured in different units. For example: PM2.5 is commonly measured in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). Ozone is commonly measured in parts per billion (ppb). The AQI converts these different measurements into a common scale for public communication. The EPA periodically updates AQI breakpoints when applicable health-based standards change. AQI and Health As AQI levels increase, the potential for adverse health effects generally increases. At moderately elevated levels, people with certain underlying health conditions may experience effects before others. At higher levels, health concerns extend to increasingly large portions of the population. How Air Pollution Affects Human Health​ The health effects of air pollution depend on the specific pollutant, concentration, duration of exposure, and individual susceptibility. Respiratory Effects Certain pollutants can irritate or inflame the respiratory system. Potential effects include: Coughing. Airway irritation. Reduced lung function. Aggravated asthma. Worsening of chronic respiratory conditions. Cardiovascular Effects Exposure to fine particulate pollution is associated with increased cardiovascular health risks. Fine particles can contribute to systemic inflammation and other biological responses. Studies have linked elevated particle exposure with increased risks of cardiovascular events, particularly among susceptible populations. Short-Term and Long-Term Exposure Short-term exposure refers to pollution experienced over hours or days. Long-term exposure refers to repeated or sustained exposure over months or years. Both can affect health, although the nature and magnitude of the effects differ. Poor Air Quality in Provo​ Provo experiences air-quality challenges associated with Utah Valley's geography and regional emissions. Three recurring conditions are especially relevant. Winter: Fine Particulate Pollution During winter, temperature inversions can trap pollution near the valley floor. The resulting buildup of PM2.5 is one of northern Utah's most significant air-quality concerns. Summer: Ground-Level Ozone Warm temperatures and strong sunlight can support the formation of ground-level ozone. Ozone levels may become elevated under favorable weather and pollution conditions. Wildfire Season: Smoke Wildfires in Utah and surrounding states can send smoke into Utah Valley. These smoke events may temporarily elevate particulate concentrations and reduce visibility. Air Quality Monitoring The Utah Division of Air Quality operates an air-monitoring network and publishes air-quality observations and forecasts. Monitoring stations measure selected pollutants, allowing agencies to evaluate changing conditions and public health concerns. Air quality can vary between locations because of elevation, emissions, terrain, and weather conditions. The 2022 Pre-Disaster Mitigation Plan identifies poor air quality as a significant regional hazard. It assigns poor air quality a High likelihood and Critical potential magnitude. A good starting point for learning how radios work is the electromagnetic spectrum. The electromagnetic spectrum organizes different forms of light by their wavelength and frequency. This includes gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet light, visible light, infrared light, microwaves, and radio waves. All forms of electromagnetic energy, including radio waves, travel at the speed of light. As you move from left to right across the spectrum above, wavelengths become longer and frequencies become lower. Compared to visible light, radio waves operate at much lower frequencies and much longer wavelengths. Wavelength, Amplitude, & Frequency Wavelength: the distance between two matching points on a wave. Amplitude: the height or magnitude of a wave. Frequency: the number of wave cycles that pass a fixed point each second. Frequency is measured in units called Hertz (Hz), which represent the number of wave cycles occurring each second. Radio frequencies span a very large range, from 3 kilohertz to 300 gigahertz. Unit Equivalent 1 Hertz (Hz) 1 cycle per second 1 Kilohertz (kHz) 1,000 cycles per second 1 Megahertz (MHz) 1,000,000 cycles per second 1 Gigahertz (GHz) 1,000,000,000 cycles per second Because wavelength and frequency affect how radio signals travel and behave, radio frequencies are often grouped into frequency ranges. In amateur radio, HF, VHF, and UHF are three of the most commonly used frequency ranges. Range Name Abbreviation Frequency Range Very Low Frequency VLF 3 kHz – 30 kHz Low Frequency LF 30 kHz – 300 kHz Medium Frequency MF 300 kHz – 3 MHz High Frequency HF 3 MHz – 30 MHz Very High Frequency VHF 30 MHz – 300 MHz Ultra High Frequency UHF 300 MHz – 3 GHz Super High Frequency SHF 3 GHz – 30 GHz Extremely High Frequency EHF 30 GHz – 300 GHz HF (High Frequency) Long-distance communication Signals can reflect off the ionosphere Larger antennas Common for regional and worldwide contacts VHF (Very High Frequency) Primarily line-of-sight communication Reliable local and regional coverage Commonly used for repeaters Includes the 2-meter amateur band UHF (Ultra High Frequency) Primarily line-of-sight communication Better building penetration Shorter communication range Includes the 70-centimeter amateur band
Radios are made up of five main components.

A transmitter generates radio waves that carry information from one location to another. When someone speaks into a radio's microphone, the transmitter converts the sound of their voice into an electrical signal. That signal is encoded onto a carrier wave and sent to the antenna where it is radiated outward as radio waves.

A receiver performs the opposite function of a transmitter. It captures incoming radio waves through the antenna and separates the information from the carrier wave. The receiver then converts that information back into usable audio or data, such as sound from a speaker or information displayed on a screen. TRANSCEIVERS Some radios only receive signals. A common example is a car radio or a police scanner. Other radios, called transceivers, can both transmit and receive signals.

An antenna allows a radio system to efficiently transmit and receive radio waves. During transmission, electrical energy is applied to the antenna, creating changing electric and magnetic fields that radiate outward as radio waves. During reception, the antenna captures radio waves from the surrounding environment and passes them to the receiver. Antenna size and design are often related to the frequency being used.

A feed line, also called a transmission line, carries the radio frequency energy between the radio equipment and the antenna. Coaxial cable is one of the most common types of feed line used in radio systems. Proper feed lines help minimize signal loss and improve overall system performance.

A power supply provides the electrical energy needed to operate the radio equipment. Radio systems may be powered by batteries, vehicle electrical systems, generators, solar systems, or external power supplies. Reliable power is essential for both transmitting and receiving radio signals.

Radio waves by themselves do not contain useful information. To send voice, data, images, or other information over radio waves, the information must first be added to a carrier wave. This process is called modulation. Different types of modulation encode information by changing specific properties of a carrier wave. Some methods vary the wave’s amplitude (strength), while others vary its frequency or phase. The type of modulation being used often determines the radio's operating mode.

Amplitude Modulation, or AM, works by changing the amplitude (strength) of the carrier wave while leaving the frequency unchanged. As the audio changes, the height of the radio wave increases and decreases to carry the information. AM signals can often travel long distances, especially on lower frequencies. Single Sideband (SSB)​ Single Sideband, or SSB, is a more efficient form of AM communication commonly used on HF amateur radio bands. SSB works by transmitting only the portion of the signal needed to carry voice information. Because less power and bandwidth are used, SSB signals can communicate over very long distances more effectively than standard AM. Most long-distance voice communication on the HF bands uses either Upper Sideband (USB) or Lower Sideband (LSB).

Frequency Modulation, or FM, works by changing the frequency of the carrier wave while the amplitude stays mostly the same. As the audio changes, the radio wave shifts slightly closer together or farther apart to carry the information. FM signals generally provide clearer audio quality and are commonly used for VHF and UHF communications.

Antenna size is closely related to wavelength and operating frequency. In general: Lower frequencies require larger antennas Higher frequencies require smaller antennas Many antennas are designed to be a fraction of the signal wavelength, such as: Quarter-wave antennas Half-wave antennas This is one reason HF antennas are often much larger than VHF or UHF antennas.

An operating mode describes the method a radio uses to communicate information. Different modes are designed for different purposes such as voice communication, digital messaging, image transmission, or long distance communication. Some modes are designed for clear local communication, while others are optimized for weak signals or efficient use of bandwidth. Operating Mode Modulation Modes Analog Voice FM, AM, SSB, PM, ISB, DSB-SC Digital AMTOR, Hellschreiver, Multi Tone 63 (MT63), MFSK (JT65, FT8 etc), Packet Radio/AX25 (AMPRNet & APRS), Phase-Shift Keying (PSK31 etc), Frequency-Shift Keying/Radioteletype (RTTY) Digital Voice DMR, D-STAR, System Fusion, P25, NXDN, M17 Image/Video Slow Scan TV (SSTV), Fast Scan TV (FSTV-NTSC standard) Morse Code Continuous Wave (CW), Modulated Continuous Wave (MCW), Frequency-Shift Keying (FSK) Procedural Activities (Modes): EchoLink, Earth-Moon-Earth (EME), Automatically Controlled Digital Stations (ACDS), OSCAR, Low transmitter power (QRP), ALS, ALE

Digital modes allow radios to transmit information such as text, images, location data, and computer-generated signals using radio waves. Instead of transmitting only voice, digital modes convert information into digital data that can be transmitted and decoded by radios, computers, or specialized equipment. Different digital modes are designed for different purposes. Some are optimized for weak-signal communication over long distances, while others are used for messaging, position reporting, emergency communications, or digital voice. Digital modes are widely used in modern amateur radio because they can often maintain usable communication in conditions where analog voice becomes noisy or difficult to understand. Popular Digital Phone Modes​ Digital phone modes transmit digitally encoded voice instead of traditional analog FM audio. These systems often provide clearer audio, identification features, messaging capabilities, and improved spectrum efficiency. Many digital voice systems also support repeater networking, allowing operators to communicate across large geographic areas using linked repeater systems or internet-connected networks. Popular digital phone modes include: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) — Widely used in amateur and commercial radio systems D-STAR — Developed by the Japan Amateur Radio League (JARL) and adopted by Icom System Fusion (C4FM) — Developed by Yaesu P25 (Project 25) — Commonly used by public safety agencies Because many digital voice systems use different protocols, radios are often only compatible with specific digital modes. APRS​ APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) is a digital modulation mode used to transmit real-time information over radio. APRS is commonly used for: Position and GPS tracking Short text messaging Weather station reporting Emergency communications Tactical location tracking during events Most APRS activity in North America occurs on 144.390 MHz using packet radio. APRS allows operators to share information with nearby stations, digipeaters, internet gateways, and mapping systems in real time.

Propagation refers to the way radio signals travel through the environment. Frequency, terrain, atmospheric conditions, obstacles, antennas, and polarization all affect how radio signals behave. Radio signals can travel in several different ways depending on the frequency and surrounding conditions. Some signals travel primarily in straight lines, while others can reflect, refract, or bend around obstacles. Understanding propagation helps radio operators choose appropriate frequencies, antennas, and operating methods for different communication situations.

Most VHF and UHF communications rely on line-of-sight propagation. Signals generally travel best when there is a clear, unobstructed path between stations. Terrain, buildings, trees, and other obstacles can block or weaken signals. Increasing antenna height often improves communication range because it extends the radio horizon. Common examples of line-of-sight communication include: Handheld radios Mobile radios Repeaters Public safety communications Most VHF and UHF amateur radio operations

Ground wave propagation occurs when radio signals follow the curvature of the earth. Lower-frequency signals, especially in the LF and MF ranges, can travel significant distances using ground wave propagation. Ground wave signals are commonly used for: AM broadcast radio Maritime communications Navigation systems Some military communications Ground conductivity, terrain, and frequency all affect ground wave performance.

Skywave propagation occurs when radio signals are refracted by the ionosphere back toward the earth. This allows some HF signals to travel hundreds or even thousands of miles beyond the horizon. Skywave propagation is strongly affected by: Time of day Solar activity Frequency Season Atmospheric conditions HF operators often use skywave propagation for long-distance communication.

Diffraction occurs when radio waves bend around obstacles such as mountains, hills, or buildings. Lower frequencies generally diffract more effectively than higher frequencies. This is one reason VHF signals often travel farther than UHF signals in mountainous terrain. Diffraction can allow communication even when stations do not have a perfect line of sight.

Reflection occurs when radio waves bounce off surfaces such as buildings, mountains, metal structures, or atmospheric layers. Reflected signals can sometimes improve communication range, but they can also create multipath interference where multiple versions of the same signal arrive at different times. Reflection is commonly observed in: Urban environments Indoor radio communications Satellite communications HF skywave propagation

Refraction occurs when radio waves bend as they pass through areas of the atmosphere with different densities or electrical properties. Atmospheric refraction can slightly extend the radio horizon beyond normal line-of-sight distances. Under certain weather conditions, signals may travel unusually long distances through tropospheric ducting.

Polarization Polarization: the orientation of the radio wave's electric field relative to the earth. Common types of polarization include: Vertical Horizontal Circular For best performance, transmitting and receiving antennas should use the same polarization. Most handheld and mobile amateur radio communications use vertical polarization because vertical antennas are practical for portable and vehicle-mounted operation. Horizontal polarization is commonly used for many HF and weak-signal communications. Circular polarization is commonly used in satellite communications because it helps compensate for changes in antenna orientation during operation. A mismatch in polarization can significantly reduce signal strength and communication quality.

Radio signals can be affected by both natural and man-made interference. Common interference sources include: Power lines Electronics Motors Atmospheric noise Buildings and terrain Interference can reduce signal quality, create static, or make communication difficult.
Simplex uses a single frequency for both transmitting and receiving. Duplex uses separate transmit and receive frequencies. This is commonly used with repeaters.

Repeaters help extend communication range. A repeater works by receiving a signal on one frequency and retransmitting it on another frequency. Separate frequencies are used because the repeater’s transmitted signal would overpower its receiver if both operated on the same frequency at the same time. Repeaters are often placed at elevated locations such as mountaintops, towers, or tall buildings to improve coverage. Many repeaters also transmit at higher power levels than handheld radios, allowing signals to travel much farther than direct radio-to-radio communication. PROGRAMMING FOR A REPEATER Input Frequency: The frequency your radio transmits on. Output Frequency: The frequency your radio listens on. Offset: The difference between repeater input and output frequencies. An offset can be positive or negative. Tone (CTCSS / PL Tone): Some repeaters require an access tone before they will retransmit a signal. If the correct tone is not used, the repeater will ignore the transmission. Access tones help prevent interference between nearby repeaters using the same frequencies or offsets. REPEATER TIPS A courtesy tone is a brief tone transmitted after a station unkeys. It indicates: The repeater is ready for the next station The previous transmission has fully cleared Listening for the courtesy tone and pausing briefly before transmitting again helps prevent doubling and allows other stations time to break in. Some repeaters remain keyed briefly after transmission ends. This is called hang time. Hang time helps conversations flow more smoothly and reduces repeated key-up delays. Many repeaters include a time-out timer to prevent excessively long transmissions. If a station transmits too long, the repeater may stop retransmitting until the timer resets. To avoid this, keep your transmissions concise.
Controls received audio level. Set the volume high enough to hear clearly without making the audio uncomfortable or distorted.

Squelch mutes background receiver noise when no signal is present. Proper squelch setting: High enough to eliminate unwanted noise Low enough to avoid blocking weak signals If squelch is set too high, weak stations may not be heard. Not all radios include squelch control.

RF Gain controls receiver sensitivity. Higher gain: Better weak-signal reception More noise may be heard Lower gain: Less interference Reduced weak-signal reception Not all radios include RF Gain control.
Mic Gain controls transmitted audio strength. Improper settings may cause: Weak audio Distorted audio Overdriven audio Use moderate settings unless adjustment is needed.

There are many different types of radios, each designed for specific uses, such as talking with family, coordinating work, or communicating during emergencies. In the United States, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) sets rules for how these radios can be used, including which frequencies are allowed and whether a license is required. This guide explains the most common radio services, what they are used for, and their frequencies. Remember, just because you can listen to a frequency does not mean you are allowed to transmit on it.

Understanding Radio Licenses: Some radio services can be used without a personal FCC license, while others require one. Certain services are limited to authorized users or organizations. Regardless of licensing requirements, you must use equipment and frequencies permitted for that service.
